articles.title: Big Five Personality Test (OCEAN) | Tool Guide
articles.excerpt: A practical guide to Big Five results: what each trait means, how trait combinations affect outcomes, and how to convert scores into concrete behavior changes.
articles.content_md:
The Big Five is best treated as a coordinate system, not a type badge. It captures your position on five continuous dimensions and helps explain stable behavior tendencies over time.

## What this assessment does
The model measures Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism as continuous traits. That keeps signal granularity and makes the output suitable for long-term tracking.

## Model logic: from input to output
Input items sample stable tendencies in cognition, motivation, social interaction, and stress reactivity. Output combines those dimensions into behavior forecasts: where you perform with lower friction, where overload is likely, and which adjustments are trainable.

## Turning scores into decisions
Use results for two tasks:
- **environment fit**: place yourself in workflows where your trait profile naturally performs;
- **skill compensation**: pick one weak link and build an external structure around it.

Example: if Conscientiousness is low, improve task decomposition and accountability before blaming willpower.

## Combination effects matter
Single scores are less useful than trait interactions. Openness × Conscientiousness affects innovation-to-delivery balance. Neuroticism × Conscientiousness affects stress resilience versus burnout risk.

## Scientific boundaries
Big Five has strong research support, but still reflects probabilistic measurement. Self-report is sensitive to context and social desirability. Use trend + behavioral evidence, not one-time numbers.

## References
[1] John, O. P., & Srivastava, S. (1999). The Big-Five trait taxonomy.
[2] Barrick, M. R., & Mount, M. K. (1991). The Big Five personality dimensions and job performance.

articles.excerpt: How to use PHQ-9/GAD-7 style screening output correctly: as symptom signal and severity tracking, not a diagnosis label.
articles.content_md:
This assessment should be used as **screening + severity quantification**. It translates hard-to-describe emotional and somatic experiences into structured signals you can communicate and track.

## What this assessment does
The tool samples symptom frequency over a recent time window (often two weeks), usually aligned with validated frameworks such as PHQ-9 and GAD-7.

## Model logic: from input to output
Input captures symptom clusters such as mood, anhedonia, sleep, energy, concentration, tension, and worry. Output maps to severity bands and helps decide action level: observe, intervene, or seek urgent professional care.

## Practical use in care pathways
Use scores to improve communication with clinicians and to monitor trend over time. Repeated measurement is especially useful when you are in treatment and need to evaluate whether recovery is stable or fluctuating with stress events.

## Critical boundary
Screening is not diagnosis. If you have suicidal ideation, self-harm risk, or immediate safety concerns, contact local emergency services or crisis support immediately.

## Ethical use
Do not use mental-health screening scores for hiring, elimination, or punitive evaluation in organizations.

A standard depression screener is an early-warning instrument. It is useful when you feel persistently “off” but cannot yet describe the pattern clearly.

## What this assessment does
The tool converts subjective discomfort into observable symptom signals, often around low mood, anhedonia, sleep, energy, appetite, concentration, and guilt/self-worth.

## Model logic: from input to output
Input samples symptom frequency across a short period. Output returns a risk/severity band to support next-step decisions: continue observation, start lifestyle intervention, or seek professional care.

## Turning score into action
Do not overfocus on a single score. Combine score with function impact: work, study, social connection, and daily self-care. If function is declining, escalation is warranted even when uncertainty remains.

## Trend > one-time result
The highest utility comes from repeated measurement and context linkage: sleep changes, stress events, physical illness, and medication shifts.

## Scientific boundaries
Screening does not equal diagnosis. Use this tool as a decision aid and communication bridge, not as a final judgment about identity or worth.

articles.title: EQ Test | Tool Guide
articles.excerpt: A practical guide to emotional intelligence measurement: what is assessed, where self-report can bias, and how to turn results into trainable behavior.
articles.content_md:
Emotional intelligence (EI/EQ) is not a single construct. Some models measure emotional ability; others measure self-reported emotional tendencies.

## What this assessment does
An EQ test typically evaluates how you identify, interpret, and regulate emotional signals in yourself and others. The first interpretation step is to confirm whether the instrument is ability-based or self-report based.

## Model logic: from input to output
Input samples emotional recognition, appraisal, regulation, and expression patterns. Output highlights likely weak links in your emotional workflow, such as delayed recognition, impulsive response, or poor need articulation.

## Turning result into skill growth
Use results as a training map, not a social label. Start with one micro-practice:
- naming emotion before reacting;
- adding a pause in conflict before response;
- expressing need without blame.

## Common misuse
“High EQ” is not people-pleasing and not manipulation skill. Healthy emotional intelligence includes boundaries, clarity, and regulation under pressure.

## Scientific boundaries
Self-report EQ can be affected by self-image bias and context. Use repeated observation and behavioral outcomes to validate progress.

## References
[1] Mayer, J. D., Salovey, P., & Caruso, D. R. (2008). Emotional intelligence: New ability or eclectic traits?
[2] Petrides, K. V., et al. (2007). Trait emotional intelligence and criterion validity.

articles.content_md:
A useful way to read IQ-style output is as a constrained cognitive signal, not as identity ranking.

## What this assessment does
Standard IQ frameworks compare your performance on structured tasks against a norm group. Online variants cannot fully reproduce controlled clinical conditions, but can still provide directional insights when design and scoring are disciplined.

## Model logic: from input to output
Input tasks often sample abstract reasoning and pattern discovery under time and complexity constraints. Output converts raw performance into standardized indicators such as percentile or score bands.

## Practical use
Use results to optimize learning/work strategy:
- choose task structure that matches your reasoning style;
- reduce avoidable performance loss through sleep, focus hygiene, and pacing.

## Common misuse
Do not treat one score as total intelligence or personal worth. Creativity, motivation, domain knowledge, and social capability are not captured by a single IQ index.

## Scientific boundaries
Treat online IQ output as trend/reference, especially when administration conditions are uncontrolled.

[1] Raven, J. C. (2000). The Raven's Progressive Matrices.
[2] Neisser, U., et al. (1996). Intelligence: Knowns and unknowns.

articles.title: MBTI Personality Test (16 Types) | Tool Guide
articles.excerpt: A practical, non-mythical guide to MBTI: what it measures, what it does not, and how to use results for better decisions in work, relationships, and self-management.
articles.content_md:
This is FermatMind's tool-level guide to MBTI. The goal is not to romanticize four letters, but to convert personality signals into reusable decision rules.

## What this assessment does
MBTI does not answer the lifetime question of “who you truly are.” It maps your default preferences across four dimensions: where you restore energy, how you collect information, how you validate decisions, and how much structure you prefer in uncertain environments.

## Model logic: from input to output
At the input layer, MBTI observes your tendency in **E/I** and **S/N**. That describes your natural channel for stimulation and pattern recognition. At the output layer, **T/F** and **J/P** describe your decision validation and execution rhythm. The dimensions are linked, not isolated.

## How to use results in real life
Use MBTI as a working hypothesis, not a label. Track three high-energy situations and three high-friction situations over two weeks. Then test one behavioral change, such as:
- changing conflict sequence from “solution first” to “emotion first, then solution”;
- reducing planning granularity from “perfect plan” to “minimum executable plan.”

## Common misuse to avoid
Two patterns create harm:
- using type as an excuse (“I am just like this”);
- using type as a weapon (classifying others instead of understanding them).

## Scientific boundaries
MBTI has practical value for communication and reflection, but also known psychometric limitations, especially around binary category cuts and retest stability near boundaries. Treat dimension strength and behavioral evidence as primary, not the type code itself.

## References
[1] Myers, I. B., McCaulley, M. H., Quenk, N. L., & Hammer, A. L. (1998). *MBTI Manual: A Guide to the Development and Use of the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator* (3rd ed.).
[2] McCrae, R. R., & Costa, P. T., Jr. (1989). Reinterpreting the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator from the perspective of the five-factor model of personality.

articles.content_md:
This is FermatMind's tool-level guide to the Enneagram. The model is most useful when it helps you observe recurring motivation loops, not when it becomes a rigid identity label.

## What this assessment does
The Enneagram describes nine recurring motivation patterns. It asks what you protect, what you avoid, and which strategy you repeat when you want safety, value, autonomy, or connection.

## How to use the result
Use your type as a working hypothesis. Track three situations where you overreacted, withdrew, overcontrolled, performed, or tried to rescue harmony. Then compare the trigger, the story you told yourself, and the behavior that followed.

## Growth boundary
A type should not become an excuse. Good Enneagram work turns a pattern into a choice: you notice the automatic move earlier, name the need underneath it, and practice one response that gives you more range.

## Scientific boundary
The Enneagram has value as a reflective framework, but it should not be treated as a diagnostic instrument or employment filter. Use it for self-observation, coaching language, and growth planning, then validate it with behavior over time.

The Enneagram becomes useful when it changes how you respond in ordinary situations. Instead of asking whether a type description sounds accurate, ask where the pattern costs you flexibility.

## Start with one loop
Pick one repeated loop: proving competence, keeping peace, staying independent, avoiding pain, or preparing for every risk. Write down the trigger, the automatic interpretation, and the protective behavior.

## Run a small experiment
Choose one behavior to soften for a week. A Type Two might ask directly instead of rescuing first. A Type Five might share an early draft before feeling fully ready. A Type Eight might state vulnerability before control.

Growth is not about acting like another type. It is about expanding range while keeping the strengths that already work. Review whether the experiment reduced friction, improved clarity, or changed how quickly you recovered from stress.

articles.title: Choosing a College Major After the Gaokao: How to Use RIASEC, MBTI, and Career Interest Tests
articles.excerpt: Before submitting Gaokao applications, use RIASEC, MBTI, and real-world exploration as inputs—not verdicts—when comparing majors. This guide explains what these tools can and cannot tell you.
articles.content_md:
## Quick Answer: How Should Tests Be Used When Choosing a Major for Gaokao Applications?

1. First examine scores, rank positions, subject requirements, enrollment plans, and admissions regulations to determine the actual range of majors you can apply to, be admitted to, and realistically pursue.
2. Use RIASEC to identify which learning tasks, work activities, and occupational environments resonate most with you—rather than letting the test dictate your major choice.
3. Use MBTI to better understand your learning style, communication preferences, decision-making approach, and collaboration tendencies; it is useful for understanding "how I learn and collaborate," but not suitable for directly answering "what major should I choose."
4. Map test results onto major course content, curriculum structure, lab/experiential requirements, future job responsibilities, and real-world tasks—not onto a specific major name.
5. Finally, validate through course syllabi, interviews with upperclassmen, open lectures, small projects, internship observations, or industry insights: are you genuinely willing to commit long-term to this major?

One-sentence summary: **Gaokao college application major selection is not "take a test and then fill out the application" but rather first narrowing down options using scores and rules, then formulating hypotheses based on career interests and personality preferences, and finally refining those hypotheses through real course work and actual tasks.**

## Who is this article for?

This article is suitable for three types of readers:

- Students: who already have a general sense of their scores or rank, but are overwhelmed by dozens of major names and unsure how to prioritize them.
- Parents: concerned that the student might only follow popular majors, peer recommendations, MBTI personality types, or employment and salary rankings when making decisions.
- Individuals who haven't received their scores yet but want to prepare in advance: who wish to take career interest tests, MBTI assessments, or other major selection tools, but don’t want to be misled by the idea that "tests determine your major."

This article does not tell you which school or major to apply to. Instead, it performs a different task: it breaks down the process of choosing a major into a clear, checkable, discussable, and verifiable workflow.

## Ask the Right Question: You Are Not Just Asking "What Major Fits Me?"

When choosing a major for Gaokao applications, families often compress several different questions into “What major suits me?” No single test can answer that. Separate the decision into these questions:

| The question you really want to ask | What to look for first | What testing can help | What testing cannot replace |
|---|---|---|---|
| Can I apply? | Score, rank, admission cutoffs, subject-combination requirements, enrollment plans, physical examination/single subject restrictions | Testing can do little to determine eligibility; it can only help order possible areas of interest | Provincial education examination authority rules, admissions regulations, and program-group requirements |
| Is this major worth studying? | Major courses, curriculum plans, graduation requirements, school resources | Help you determine which courses and tasks are more worthy of in-depth understanding | Official major catalog, the institution's official curriculum, real course information |
| Would I be interested in it? | Course content, experiments/projects, future work activities | RIASEC can help observe work activities and preferred work environments | Long-term learning experience, project feedback, internship experience |
| Does my learning style match? | Teaching methods, assignment formats, teamwork, expression requirements | MBTI can be used as a reference for learning and communication preferences | Learning ability, examination performance, admission outcomes |
| Is this direction realistically feasible? | City, tuition fees, family constraints, rules for changing majors, employment information | Help you ask questions to be verified | Family decisions, provincial policies, real changes in the job market |


- Which majors am I eligible to apply for given my rank, selected subjects, health requirements, and the official admissions plan?
- Which core courses and training methods can I realistically sustain?
- Which kinds of learning tasks and future work activities am I willing to explore?
- What constraints involving tuition, city, program length, and family circumstances matter?
- Which assumptions can I test through course materials, open classes, interviews, or a small project?
- Which options should be retained, verified further, or temporarily excluded?

Tests can help generate questions at the interest and preference layers. They cannot override official eligibility rules or provide an admissions decision.

## Why Not Choose a Major Based Only on Popularity, Parental Advice, or MBTI?

Each source of advice can contribute information, but none should decide the major by itself.


Popularity should be translated into evidence about curriculum and real tasks. Parents’ concerns should be written as constraints to verify. Test results should become questions—not labels.

## How to Choose a Major: What Are the Hard Requirements?

Before any testing, first examine the eligibility requirements. Eligibility requirements are not romantic—they determine whether you're eligible to apply, whether admission is even possible, and whether you can actually enroll and study there.

It's recommended to gather information from these 8 categories:

1. **Scores and Rank**: The meaning of a score varies across years; ranks generally provide a more useful reference point than raw scores when establishing a range.
2. **Batch cutoffs and admission rules**: Admission criteria differ by province, batch, and program group—rules cannot be directly transferred from other provinces.
3. **Subject requirements**: Especially in new Gaokao regions, it’s essential to confirm specific subject prerequisites—for example, physics, chemistry, or biology—required for certain program groups or majors.
4. **Enrollment plans**: Review the number of available spots within your own province—not just the prestige of the university.
5. **Admission regulations**: Pay attention to restrictions such as individual subject scores, language proficiency, physical examination, additional exams, and major reassignment policies.
6. Major course requirements: Examine core courses taken during the first three years—not just the name of the major.
7. **Training methods**: Assess the proportion of experimental work, internships, thesis writing, projects, competitions, and practical classes.
8. **School resources and transfer mechanisms**: Evaluate faculty and institutional support, guaranteed admission/transfer policies, cross-disciplinary opportunities, and local industrial ecosystem.

At this stage, the value of career interest assessments and MBTI is not to "screen" universities for you—it's instead to help you ask more specific questions: Which types of coursework should I prioritize? What kinds of learning tasks am I most likely to engage with? Which majors sound appealing but have curricula I might resist in practice?

## RIASEC Career Interest Assessment

RIASEC is most useful after clearly ineligible options have been removed. It helps you ask which learning and work activities deserve closer investigation.

| RIASEC signal | Possible tips when choosing a major | What should be checked | What conclusions should not be drawn directly |
|---|---|---|---|
| Realistic (R) is relatively high | May be more interested in specific systems, equipment, engineering, operations, and practical tasks | Proportion of experimental classes, practical training, engineering projects, and on-site practice | "I can only study engineering" |
| Investigative (I) is relatively high | May be willing to analyze problems, do research, and understand system causes | Mathematics/statistics/experiment/scientific research training intensity | "I must be suitable for scientific research" |
| Artistic (A) is relatively high | May value expression, creation, open questions and design space | Portfolio, design classes, presentation-based projects, creative training | "I can only study art majors" |
| Social (S) is relatively high | May care more about education, help, communication and feedback | Internship settings, work serving people, teaching/consulting/organizing activities | "All humanities and social sciences are suitable for me" |
| Enterprising (E) is relatively high | May be more sensitive to influence, organization, business, resource coordination and result feedback | Business projects, management courses, competitions, organizational practice | "I must study business" |
| Conventional (C) is relatively high | May like structure, order, data, processes and reliable execution | Accounting, data, rules, processes, operations courses | "I am not suitable for innovative majors" |


Use the strongest and weakest activity preferences to select majors for further course and task verification. Do not map a RIASEC code directly to one “correct” major.

## What Can MBTI Offer When Choosing a Major?

MBTI-style language may help you compare learning and decision preferences:

| MBTI Observation Points | How it helps in choosing a major | Risks | Safer ways to ask |
|---|---|---|---|
| Information processing preferences | Determine your comfort level when facing abstract theories, cases, data, and experiments | Treat S/N as intelligence level | Is the core course of this major mainly concepts, experiments, cases, or projects? |
| Decision-making preferences | Understand the way you deal with value conflicts, logical judgments and interpersonal influences | Treat T/F as a ranking of rationality versus emotion | Is this major curriculum more focused on rule-based reasoning, policy judgment, or communication with people? |
| Collaboration preference | Observe your own energy consumption in group assignments, presentations, and internships | Treat E/I as social skills | How much presentation, communication, and teamwork is required for this major? |
| Life organization preferences | Determine how you adapt to open tasks, deadlines, and structured courses | Use J/P as a self-discipline/procrastination label | Are the assignments and projects in this major spread across the term or concentrated in short bursts? |


- Do you prefer to think privately before discussion, or develop ideas through interaction?
- Are you drawn first to concrete cases and details, or to concepts and possibilities?
- Do you prioritize consistent criteria, or begin with people and values affected by a decision?
- Do you work better with early structure, or with room to revise as information changes?

A safer approach is to turn each preference into two competing study strategies and test both. For example, compare reading the conceptual overview before examples with studying worked examples before the overview. The result can inform learning experiments, but it cannot determine eligibility, capability, or major outcomes.

## Should you consider the Big Five personality?

The Big Five is not the main focus of this article, but it can serve as a third-level reference. It is better suited for observing long-term behavioral tendencies, such as Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Emotional Stability. For more on the OCEAN five dimensions, see [What is the Big Five personality test?](/en/articles/big-five-tool-guide).

In Gaokao college application decisions, the Big Five is more useful for asking:

- What kind of rhythm support do I need when facing long-term tasks?
- How sensitive am I to uncertainty and stress?
- Do I require frequent social feedback, or am I better suited to independent, deep work?
- To what extent am I open to new fields, new courses, and interdisciplinary exploration?

However, the Big Five cannot determine a major nor predict personal career success. It can only help you identify learning support systems earlier.

## The Roles of RIASEC, MBTI, and the Big Five in Major Selection


Official admissions rules, rank, subject requirements, curriculum facts, cost, and real-world validation remain separate evidence layers.

| Tool | What is the main answer | Suitable for use in the chosen major | Not suitable for use | Safer usage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Holland / RIASEC | Which work activities and major environments am I more attracted to? | Prioritize the major tasks and future work environment worth studying | Decide on majors, predict admissions, predict employment | Generate a list of "Which major tasks do I want to verify?" |
| MBTI | How do I learn, communicate, make decisions, and collaborate? | Understand major learning methods and team collaboration experience | Select majors directly by type | Assess whether the major's courses and project formats would be sustainable for you over time |
| Big Five Personality | What are my long-term behavioral tendencies and stress boundaries? | Design learning support systems and observe stress sources | Determine ability or career success | Anticipate learning pace, feedback methods and adaptation conditions |
| Official application information | Can I apply, how to apply, and what rules apply? | Confirm scores, ranks, subject-combination requirements, enrollment plans, and restrictions in admissions regulations | Be replaced by any assessment | Use it as the final authority for the formal application |
| Real-world verification | Am I willing to continue investing in this direction? | Test hypotheses through courses, interviews, projects, and internships | Be replaced by a single assessment result | Put interests and preferences into real tasks to test |


## What If Your RIASEC and MBTI Results Do Not Match?

Apparent disagreement is expected because the tools ask different questions.

| Situation | What it may mean | How not to interpret | Next step to verify |
|---|---|---|---|
| RIASEC points to research/technology, MBTI shows a greater need for discussion and external feedback | You may be suitable for a study/work environment with analytical depth, but not completely isolated | "I am not suitable for research-oriented majors" | Looking for research-based courses that require presentations, team discussions or application scenarios |
| RIASEC points toward Social or education-related activities, MBTI shows that you need a lot of independent time | You may care about people, but are not suitable for high-frequency emotional labor | "I am not suitable for people-related majors" | Compare how much and what kind of interpersonal contact is involved in education, consulting, public services, content design, and similar fields. |
| RIASEC interests are scattered and MBTI results do not show a strong pattern | You may lack real major exposure and cannot judge for the time being | "I am not interested" | Do 3 low-cost course/project experiences first |
| MBTI is clear, but RIASEC is not obvious | You know how to study, but you don’t know what tasks you want to learn yet | “Just choose by MBTI” | Use RIASEC or a course list to identify the work and learning tasks that interest you |
| RIASEC is clear, but parents expect the opposite | Interest clues and family constraints conflict | “The test said it, so parents must be wrong” | Use curriculum, employment information, school resources and cost risks to discuss together |


Do not decide which result is “correct.” Use the difference to design a more precise course, task, or environment check.

## A More Stable Major Selection Process: Scores, Majors, Interests, Real-World Validation

Gaokao college application major selection can follow a 6-step process:

1. **Eligibility Screening**: Score, rank, subject requirements, enrollment plans, batch rules, physical examination requirements, and single-subject restrictions.  
2. **Initial Major Screening List**: Compile a list of 10–20 potential majors from the available options; avoid focusing solely on 2–3 popular-sounding names at the outset.  
3. **Curriculum Breakdown**: Investigate core courses, curriculum programs, lab/practice requirements, and graduation criteria.  
4. **Test-Assisted Ranking**: Use RIASEC to assess task interests, and MBTI to evaluate learning and collaboration preferences.  
5. **Real-World Validation**: Validate through public lectures, course syllabi, interviews with upperclassmen, project experiences, and industry interviews.  
6. **Application Choice Prioritization**: Rank choices by university level, city, family cost, risk tolerance, transfer policies, and official information.

The key to this process is sequence. Do not let interest tests determine your major choice in Step 1, nor should you overlook official rules in the final step.

## From Test Results to Major Verification Checklist

The value of a test result is the quality of the questions it helps you ask.

| Test signals | Possible prompts | What major information should be checked | What should be done to verify reality | Direct conclusions are prohibited |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Investigative (I) is relatively high | More interested in analysis, experiments, and system causes | Does the major have mathematics, statistics, experiments, and research methods courses | Listen to an introductory class and do a small analysis task | "I must be suitable for scientific research" |
| Social (S) is relatively high | More sensitive to help, education, communication, and feedback from people | Whether the major has a lot of contact with people, internships, interviews, teaching or services | Interviews with seniors to understand the true emotional labor and communication intensity | "I am suitable for all liberal arts/social sciences" |
| Enterprising (E) is relatively high | Interested in organization, impact, business feedback and result orientation | Does this field involve business analysis, management, operations, or project work? | Participate in a competition/community project/business case analysis | "I must study business" |
| MBTI suggests a preference for clear structure | It may be necessary to clarify the course path and deadlines | Is the curriculum plan clear and the course highly open | Compare the types of coursework and assessment methods | "Open majors are definitely not suitable for me" |
| MBTI suggests a preference for exploration and discussion | May need discussion, feedback and interdisciplinary space | Are there seminars, project-based courses, cross-department course selection | Attend open classes or interview current students about their learning experiences | "Traditional classrooms are definitely not suitable for me" |
| Higher stress sensitivity in the Big Five | May need clearer pacing and support systems | Sources of major stress, exam density, elimination mechanisms | Understand real class schedules, homework loads, and senior year feedback | "I can't take a challenging major" |


## Common Mistakes: These Will Bias Your Testing

- Treating a test result as a direct list of recommended majors.
- Looking only at the highest code or type while ignoring weak or conflicting evidence.
- Using MBTI preferences as proof of ability.
- Treating a popular or newly named major as evidence of future demand.
- Letting one parent, teacher, influencer, or test replace official admissions facts.
- Reading the major name without checking core courses, projects, and graduation requirements.
- Using a single result to predict admission, salary, employment, or career success.
- Skipping real-world verification because a description “sounds like me.”

| Unsafe shortcut | Why it's dangerous | Safer approach |
|---|---|---|
| Select only by popular majors | Popularity does not mean that the course is suitable, nor does it mean that you will have a good job in the future | Check courses, curriculum plans, employment destinations and your own work interests |
| Only choose according to parents' recommendations | Parents may be more familiar with the risks, but they may not necessarily understand your learning experience | Put the stability, city, and cost that your parents care about together with your interests in the table |
| Select only by MBTI | MBTI is not an aptitude test, nor a major matching tool | Use it to understand learning and collaboration preferences, not to determine majors |
| Select only by Holland results | RIASEC is an interest clue, not an admission and employment prediction | Convert the results to a major verification checklist |
| Only look at the employment salary list | Salary lists often ignore individual differences, regions, academic qualifications, and industry cycles | Also look at course investment, industry paths, school resources, and personal constraints |
| Don’t read the course content | Major names are easy to mislead, what really affects the four-year experience is the curriculum and training methods | Check core courses, experimental courses, graduation requirements and project requirements |
| Not looking at the subject-combination requirements | It may lead to the inability to apply for the major at all or the range of options is greatly reduced | Look at the province, major group and school admission regulations first |
| Not doing reality verification | It is easy to regard the imaginary major as the real major | Doing open classes, interviews, small projects, and internship observations |


## After Testing, How Do You Verify Whether a Major Is Worth Applying For?

You can use this "major reality verification checklist":

1. Review the core courses of the major—not just the name of the major.
2. Check the curriculum plan and graduation requirements to see what you're actually trained in over four years.
3. Examine subject requirements, enrollment plans, and admissions regulations to confirm whether eligibility criteria are met.
4. Interview 2–3 real senior students, faculty members, or industry professionals.
5. Take a public lecture, an introductory project, or a sample course assignment to experience the actual workload of the major.
6. Note whether you feel more interested, more resistant, more fatigued, or willing to dive deeper.
7. Then combine these insights with your score rank, university level, city location, family constraints, major-transfer policies, and employment information for final decision-making.

Test hypotheses through reality verification to filter assumptions. Final application decisions must still be based on information from each province's examination authority, the Sunshine Gaokao, official admission rules, subject requirements, and score rankings. FermatMind is not an official college application system and does not predict admission outcomes.

## How should parents and students divide responsibilities effectively?

College application major choices are often not an individual decision, but a joint family decision. The most common point of conflict is that parents tend to focus on risk, while students prioritize interest or personal feelings. Neither side should be overlooked.

| Decision-making tasks | Who is more suitable to take the lead | Why | Outputs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Organizing scores, rankings, and admissions plans | The student and parents together | Need to be accurate, patient, and avoid missing conditions | Fillable major scope form |
| Course experience and interest judgment | Student-led | The next four years will be the student's actual learning experience | Course-interest ratings |
| Cost, city, family constraints | Parents participate | Involving family resources and risk tolerance | Realistic constraints list |
| Major interviews | Student-led, parents assist in finding resources | Can directly change the understanding of majors | Interview records |
| Final application preference order | Shared decision-making | Need to balance rules, interests, risks and resources | Draft application preference order |


The worst approach is: parents say only "this is stable," and the student says only "I don't like it." A better approach is: both parties review the same major verification chart together.

## What to Do Next

If you currently have no clear direction, start with the [RIASEC career interest assessment](/en/tests/holland-career-interest-test-riasec?entry_surface=article_detail_seo_cta&source_page_type=article_detail&source_route_family=article&source_slug=college-major-choice-holland-mbti-career-test&content_id=52&target_action=seo_cta_cms_content_holland_career_interest_test_riasec&test_slug=holland-career-interest-test-riasec&target_test_slug=holland-career-interest-test-riasec&cta_id=cms_content_holland_career_interest_test_riasec&landing_path=%2Fen%2Farticles%2Fcollege-major-choice-holland-mbti-career-test&entrypoint=seo_cta) and convert the results into 3–5 major interest areas worth further exploration.

 
If you already have several major candidates but are unsure whether you're suited to these learning styles, take the [MBTI Personality Test](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types?entry_surface=article_detail_seo_cta&source_page_type=article_detail&source_route_family=article&source_slug=college-major-choice-holland-mbti-career-test&content_id=52&target_action=seo_cta_cms_content_mbti_personality_test_16_personality_types&test_slug=mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types&target_test_slug=mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types&cta_id=cms_content_mbti_personality_test_16_personality_types&landing_path=%2Fen%2Farticles%2Fcollege-major-choice-holland-mbti-career-test&entrypoint=seo_cta) to observe your preferences in learning, communication, and decision-making.

If you've taken multiple tests but the results conflict, first read [Differences Between Career Interest Tests and Personality Tests](/en/articles/career-interest-vs-personality-test-differences), then read [What to Do When MBTI and RIASEC Results Don't Align](/en/articles/mbti-vs-holland-career-choice).

If you are not a Gaokao student but have entered college or are working and still feeling uncertain about your career path, consider reading [A Test and Reality Validation Map for Career Confusion](/en/articles/career-confusion-test-map).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can Major Selection for College Admissions Rely on Tests?

No. Testing can only help you explore hypotheses, such as which types of courses, tasks, or work environments you might prefer. Formal major selection still requires consideration of percentile rankings, subject requirements, enrollment plans, admission regulations, course content, family constraints, and real-world validation.

### How does the RIASEC career interest assessment help in choosing a major?

RIASEC can help you identify the types of work activities and occupational environments that most attract you. When choosing a major, it is best used to generate a list of "major tasks I should focus on studying," rather than providing direct major recommendations.

### Can MBTI be used to choose a university major?

It can serve as a supplementary reference but is not suitable on its own for major selection. MBTI is more appropriate for observing learning styles, communication approaches, decision-making preferences, and collaboration patterns. It cannot assess ability nor predict admission, employment, or career success.

### What If Your RIASEC and MBTI Results Do Not Match?

Don't jump to conclusions about who is right or wrong. RIASEC assesses interest in work activities and occupational environments, while MBTI examines preferences in learning, communication, and decision-making. When results differ, translate them into two questions: What tasks would I like to learn? How do I best learn and collaborate? Then validate through coursework, interviews, and projects.

### Should you look at scores, ranks, subject requirements, or interest tests first?

First consider scores, rank positions, subject requirements, enrollment plans, and admission regulations, as these determine whether you are eligible to apply, have a chance of admission, and meet the requirements upon admission. Interest tests should be used optionally for ranking and validation purposes, not as a substitute for eligibility criteria.

### Can career interest tests predict my future employment?

No. Career interest assessments can help you identify interest areas and preferences for work activities, but they cannot predict employment, income, promotions, or career success. Employment outcomes are also influenced by school resources, individual abilities, industry cycles, location, internship experiences, and opportunities.

### After completing tests, how do you verify whether a major is worth applying for?

First convert test results into 3–5 potential major directions, then investigate core courses, curriculum plans, subject requirements, career pathways, and actual student experiences. Attend at least one open house session, conduct one interview with upperclassmen or peer students, or engage in a low-cost project before deciding whether to include it on the application choices list.

### Is FermatMind an official college application system?

No. FermatMind provides tools for self-awareness and career interest exploration and is not an official college application system operated by Sunshine Gaokao, the Ministry of Education, CHSI (China Higher Education Student Information and Career Center), or any provincial examination institute. It also does not provide admission predictions. Official applications should still be made through authorized platforms, admissions guidelines, and rules established by each provincial examination institute.

## Keep Moving Forward

If you want to turn "I don't know what major to choose" into a discussable list, start with the [RIASEC career interest assessment](/en/tests/holland-career-interest-test-riasec?entry_surface=article_detail_seo_cta&source_page_type=article_detail&source_route_family=article&source_slug=college-major-choice-holland-mbti-career-test&content_id=52&target_action=seo_cta_cms_content_holland_career_interest_test_riasec&test_slug=holland-career-interest-test-riasec&target_test_slug=holland-career-interest-test-riasec&cta_id=cms_content_holland_career_interest_test_riasec&landing_path=%2Fen%2Farticles%2Fcollege-major-choice-holland-mbti-career-test&entrypoint=seo_cta), then convert your interest results into major validation questions.

If you already know a few directions, but want to understand your learning and collaboration preferences, take the [MBTI Personality Test](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types?entry_surface=article_detail_seo_cta&source_page_type=article_detail&source_route_family=article&source_slug=college-major-choice-holland-mbti-career-test&content_id=52&target_action=seo_cta_cms_content_mbti_personality_test_16_personality_types&test_slug=mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types&target_test_slug=mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types&cta_id=cms_content_mbti_personality_test_16_personality_types&landing_path=%2Fen%2Farticles%2Fcollege-major-choice-holland-mbti-career-test&entrypoint=seo_cta).

Remember: The test is not the answer; it's a tool to clarify your questions. What truly determines the ordering of application choices is eligibility requirements, course understanding, real-world validation, and shared family decisions.

articles.content_md:
## Quick Answer: After Scores Are Released, If There Are Too Many Majors Available, Don't Immediately Ask "What Major Is Right for Me?"

1. **Don't ask yourself "What major am I suited for?"** The first step after receiving scores is not to take a personality test, but to eliminate majors that are impossible to apply for, carry high risk, or are clearly unworthy of further consideration—based on rank position, subject requirements, enrollment plans, health/individual subject limits, and admissions regulations.
2. **Convert interests into task-based questions using RIASEC**: Do I genuinely want to engage in these tasks over the long term? — analysis, experimentation, creation, communication, organization, process management, data handling, and fieldwork?
3. **Use MBTI only as an auxiliary tool**: It can help you understand your learning style, communication preferences, and decision-making tendencies—but it cannot directly translate any 16-type personality into a specific university major.
4. **Course validation determines keeping or removing an option**: Major names, popular narratives, or newly introduced majors are insufficient. You must examine core courses, curriculum design, assignment formats, practical components, and actual work demands.
5. **Final output is a checklist**: Retain, pending verification, temporarily exclude. Test hypotheses through assessments; validate them against real-world conditions. When formally applying, always follow official guidelines from provincial education examination institutes, the Sunshine Gaokao system, school admission policies, and the official application choice platform.

This article is not "AI helping you choose a major." It's a practical, actionable major elimination list that you can immediately implement after receiving your scores.

## The 2026 Context: Start With Official Information

The Ministry of Education announced that the 2026 Gaokao Cloud Consultation Week would run on the Sunshine Gaokao information platform from June 22 through June 28. Treat that platform, provincial examination authorities, university admissions regulations, subject requirements, and official application systems as the primary sources for current admissions information.

The Ministry of Education also published the *Undergraduate Major Catalogue (2026)*, including new entries such as embodied intelligence and brain-machine science and technology. A newly listed major is still a prompt to examine course content, training conditions, and current institutional requirements; it is not evidence that the major will suit a particular student.

Newness does not determine suitability, popularity does not determine value, and an income narrative does not guarantee long-term viability. In an information-heavy application season, first remove options that do not meet your real constraints instead of collecting more major names.
## Eliminate These Six Categories First—Do Not Spend Time on Invalid Options

Temporarily remove these six categories from the main shortlist:

| Categories of majors to remove first | Why remove them first | Basis for judgment | Mistakes not to make |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Eligibility requirements are not met | If you are ineligible for a major, interest alone cannot make it a viable application option | Subject-combination requirements, physical examination restrictions, single subject requirements, enrollment plans, batch rules | Do not spend hours researching a major before checking eligibility |
| 2. Persistent aversion to core courses | The name may appeal to you, but the curriculum shapes the four-year experience | Curriculum plan, core courses, graduation requirements, assignment form | Only look at the name of the major, not the course |
| 3. I only like the name but don’t know what to study | The imagination brought by the name often deviates from the real training | Freshman and sophomore courses, experiments/practical training/papers/programming/presentation requirements | Treat “sounding advanced” as suitable |
| 4. Chosen only because it is popular, new, or associated with high pay | Popular directions usually also mean thresholds, competition and changes | Subject foundation, school resources, city opportunities, industry fluctuations | Treat trends as a guarantee |
| 5. Clear conflict with family constraints | An application must account for cost and what the family can realistically sustain, not interest alone | Tuition fees, city, accommodation, transportation, family support, risks of repeating/changing majors | Treating realistic constraints as "not idealistic enough" |
| 6. No practical way to verify the choice | Choices that cannot be verified are easily inflated by imagination | Open classes, course syllabus, senior interviews, project samples, internship tasks | Make decisions based only on short videos and relatives’ suggestions |


1. **Eligibility requirements are not met.** Selected subjects, physical-exam rules, language requirements, single-subject thresholds, or local admissions rules make the option unavailable.
2. **Core courses trigger sustained resistance.** The concern is not that a course looks difficult, but that the student is unwilling to engage with the program’s central learning tasks over time.
3. **The name is attractive but the curriculum is not.** The student likes the label or imagined lifestyle without understanding the actual training.
4. **The option is supported only by a popularity narrative.** “New,” “hot,” and “future-facing” are not substitutes for curriculum and task evidence.
5. **It conflicts with non-negotiable family constraints.** Tuition, city, program length, health, or caregiving responsibilities may make the option unrealistic.
6. **There is no practical way to verify the assumption.** If no official curriculum, task sample, interview, or low-cost experience can be found, the option needs evidence before it consumes shortlist space.

“Temporarily exclude” is reversible. Reconsider an option when new official information or credible task evidence becomes available.

## Within 30 Minutes of Seeing Your Scores: Create a Major Exclusion List

You need an updateable evidence table, not a perfect answer.

| Major name | Eligibility: rank, subject combination, enrollment plan, medical-examination rules, and single-subject requirements | What makes the name attractive | Potential core-course deal-breaker | RIASEC corresponding tasks | Issues that need to be verified | Current status | Next action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Example: Data Science | Whether the ranking is within the scope of discussion; whether physics/mathematics foundation is required | "Data", "AI", "wide range of employment" | Advanced mathematics, linear algebra, probability and statistics, programming, modeling | Investigative (I), Conventional (C), and partly Realistic (R) | Can I accept long-term mathematics and coding training? | To be verified | Look at the curriculum plan and try a Python/statistics open class |
| Example: Psychology | Is there any subject-combination requirement restriction; does the school favor teacher education, medicine, or science | "Understanding people" and "feeling helpful" | Statistics, experimental psychology, measurement, paper reading | Social (S) and Investigative (I) | Do I like to study people, or just chat? | To be verified | Check core courses and interview undergraduate psychology students |
| Example: Journalism and Communication | Is the enrollment plan and school platform sufficient | "Expression", "Media" and "Content" | News writing, communication theory, data communication, interviews, internships | Artistic (A), Social (S), and Enterprising (E) | Can I accept open feedback and high-paced output? | To be verified | See student works and internship requirements |
| Example: Mechanical/Automation | Subject-combination requirement, physical examination, school engineering platform | "Engineering", "Manufacturing", "Intelligence" | Mechanics, circuits, control, drawing, experiments, engineering projects | Realistic (R) and Investigative (I) | Am I willing to be exposed to specific systems and engineering constraints? | Needs verification | Check experimental courses and graduation projects |
| Example: Business Administration | Is it within the optional major group | "General", "Management", "Business" | Accounting, operations, organization, market, case analysis | Enterprising (E), Conventional (C), and Social (S) | Do I want to study management, or do I simply not know what to choose for the time being? | To be verified | Check the course structure and compare accounting/marketing/information management directions |


Apply three rules:

1. If a hard requirement fails, temporarily exclude the option immediately.
2. If eligibility is satisfied but course or task evidence is missing, mark it “verify.”
3. Retain an option only when the current evidence supports further investigation; retained does not mean “final choice.”

## Layer 1: Check Eligibility Requirements First—Tests Cannot Override Rules


Interest and personality assessments begin only after these conditions are checked. They cannot create eligibility where the official rules do not.

| Question | What to check first | What to do if not satisfied | What can the test do here |
|---|---|---|---|
| Is the ranking within the discussion range? | The official score-to-rank table, admissions from previous years, changes in this year’s plans | Do not enter the main list, only put it in the observation area | Basically cannot help |
| Does your subject combination meet the requirements? | School admissions regulations, subject-combination requirements, major group requirements | Exclude the option if the requirement is not met | Cannot be bypassed |
| Are there any physical examination/single subject restrictions? | Admission regulations, physical examination requirements, special major instructions | If not met, exclude or be cautious | Cannot replace official requirements |
| Is the enrollment plan too small? | This year’s enrollment plan, major composition | Mark risks, do not need to rule them out immediately | Can only assist in discussing interests |
| Are the family constraints manageable? | City, cost, accommodation, transportation, risk tolerance | Mark for verification or exclusion | Not a substitute for family decision-making |


## Layer 2: Turn Interests into "Task Problems" with RIASEC

If you need a refresher on the model, read [What Is the RIASEC Career Interest Assessment?](/en/articles/riasec-holland-career-interest-test-explained). In this checklist, use RIASEC only to form task questions:

| RIASEC Signals of Interest | Convert to Major Verification Questions | What to Check | Safer Conclusions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Realistic (R) | Does this major have specific systems, equipment, experiments, engineering, or field tasks? | Experimental courses, practical training courses, graduation projects, project-based courses | Prioritize verifying the specific tasks involved |
| Investigative (I) | Does this major require analysis, modeling, reasoning, experimentation, or data processing? | Mathematics/Statistics/Thesis/Experimental Requirements | See if you are willing to engage in long-term abstract training |
| Artistic (A) | Does this major have expression, design, content, works, or open questions? | Portfolio requirements, presentation-based classes, and creative assignments | It does not mean that you can only choose art |
| Social (S) | Does this major involve sustained work with people through teaching, service, communication, or support? | Who is served in practice, the communication load, and the emotional labor involved | See whether the "people-facing work" is real and acceptable |
| Enterprising (E) | Does this major involve organizing resources, persuading others, advancing projects, and tracking results? | Case classes, competitions, presentations, business projects | Does not necessarily mean studying business |
| Conventional (C) | Does this profession value process, data, discipline, accuracy, and order? | Accounting, auditing, statistics, data governance, documentation requirements | See if you are willing to handle structured tasks |


For each retained major, write two tasks you want to try and two you may resist. Then verify them with coursework, project descriptions, interviews, or a small task.

## Layer 3: MBTI Looks Only at Learning and Decision Preferences, Not for Direct Major Selection

For a model overview, read [What Is the MBTI Personality Test?](/en/articles/mbti-basics). If MBTI and RIASEC appear inconsistent, use [What to Do When MBTI and RIASEC Results Disagree](/en/articles/mbti-vs-holland-career-choice) to turn the difference into verification questions. MBTI-style preferences can help you compare study approaches, not majors:

| MBTI Clues | How to Use in Major Screening | What Not to Use |
|---|---|---|
| Information processing preferences | Determine whether you are more likely to learn from cases, data, concepts, or system frameworks | Infer that a given type "should study" a particular major |
| Decision-making preferences | Help you identify whether you value logic, impact, value or executability when making trade-offs | Predict future achievements |
| Communication preferences | Evaluate whether a large number of group assignments, presentations, and discussion sessions may be draining on you | Determine the level of social skills |
| Structural preferences | Observe whether you can adapt to open projects, ambiguous tasks and uncertain deadlines | Judge self-discipline or ability |


- Do you understand a topic better through concrete examples or conceptual maps?
- Do you prefer discussing an unfinished idea or thinking privately before presenting it?
- Do you make progress with an early plan or with staged checkpoints that allow revision?
- In group work, what balance of independent work and interaction is sustainable?

Turn the answers into reversible study experiments. Do not use a type to claim that someone has or lacks the ability for medicine, engineering, law, communication, or any other major.

## Layer 4: The Curriculum Is More Informative Than the Major's Name

For each program, inspect:

| Information to check | What to review | Warning sign |
|---|---|---|
| Curriculum plan | Four-year course structure, credit distribution, practical requirements | The name is very new, but the courses and resources are very vague |
| Core courses | Main courses from freshman to junior year | A large share of the core curriculum is something you would persistently resist |
| Assignment form | Exams, papers, experiments, code, presentations, group projects | A very high proportion of tasks you hate |
| School resources | Laboratories, internship bases, industry cooperation, teacher orientation | A popular-sounding major with weak supporting resources |
| Paths to further education/employment | Common destinations, job tasks, and industry changes | Salary rankings are visible, but the actual work is not |


The same major name can represent different training at different institutions. Use the target program’s official curriculum.

## Layer 5: Use Three Categories Instead of Forcing a Single Top Choice


The goal is not to name one perfect major immediately. It is to reduce an unmanageable list into a transparent decision set.

| Status | Criteria | What do you do next |
|---|---|---|
| Keep | Eligibility requirements can be discussed; core courses are acceptable; RIASEC tasks are interesting; realistic constraints can be tolerated | Compare application tiers and institutions |
| To be verified | Eligibility requirements can be discussed, but courses, tasks or realistic constraints are uncertain | Check the curriculum plan, ask seniors, try open classes or projects |
| Temporarily excluded | Eligibility requirements are not met; core courses are resisted for a long time; only the name is attractive; cannot be verified | Removed from the main list unless new evidence is obtained later |


## How to Address Conflicts When Parental Advice, Popular Narratives, and Interests Clash?


Do not settle the dispute by choosing a winner. Assign an evidence task to each disputed claim.

| Conflict situation | What it may mean | How not to argue | More effective verification actions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Parents recommend a stable major, but your interests tend to be creative/research | Parents focus on risks, you focus on task interests | "You don't understand me" / "You are too idealistic" | Write stability, courses, employment paths, and interesting tasks in the table |
| You like popular majors, but the red lines in the courses are obvious | What you like is narrative, not necessarily the training process | "Popular majors have a future" | Look at the core courses and try an introductory course |
| The Holland result supports a certain direction, but the ranking range does not | Interest is established, but the current application conditions may not support it | "The test said I am suitable" | Explore adjacent majors, minors, official major-transfer options, and postgraduate pathways |
| MBTI preferences are inconsistent with major tasks | This is just a reminder at the level of learning/communication preferences | "This type cannot learn this" | See if the course format and real assignments are adaptable |


## Common Mistakes That Make the Shortlist More Confusing

- Starting with a personality label before checking official eligibility.
- Treating rank as a guarantee rather than one input to application strategy.
- Choosing a major by name without reading the target curriculum.
- Equating “new” or “popular” with low risk or guaranteed employment.
- Treating temporary difficulty as permanent inability—or ignoring sustained resistance to central tasks.
- Letting a test directly recommend a major.
- Keeping every option “just in case” without naming the missing evidence.
- Assuming transfer to another major will definitely be available later.
- Predicting admission, salary, or career success from an interest or personality result.

| What's wrong | Why it's dangerous | What's safer |
|---|---|---|
| Select only by popular majors | Popularity does not mean suitable, nor does it mean that your school has strong resources | Check courses, school resources and real job tasks |
| Choose only from parents' recommendations | May ignore the long-term demands of studying the subject | Write the risks that parents care about into verifiable conditions |
| Select only by MBTI | MBTI is not a major recommendation tool | Only use it to supplement learning and decision-making preferences |
| Select only based on Holland results | RIASEC does not judge admissions, abilities, or employment | Convert results into task verification questions |
| Only look at the employment salary list | Income is affected by city, school, ability, and industry cycle | Check courses, internships, employment directions and job tasks |
| Don’t look at the course content | You may spend four years learning content that you have resisted for a long time | Look at the curriculum plan and core courses |
| Don’t look at the subject-combination requirements | You may not be able to apply at all | Check the official admissions regulations and subject-combination requirements first |
| No reality verification | It is easy to submit application preferences based on an imagined version of the major | Complete at least one form of verification: an open class, interview, project, or task sample |


## Next Step: Turn Test Results into Verification Questions

If your current major pool is still quite disorganized, we recommend taking this path:

1. First, eliminate majors that do not meet the official eligibility criteria.  
2. Then take the [RIASEC career interest assessment](/en/tests/holland-career-interest-test-riasec?entry_surface=article_detail_seo_cta&source_page_type=article_detail&source_route_family=article&source_slug=gaokao-score-major-shortlist-riasec-checklist&content_id=53&target_action=seo_cta_cms_content_holland_career_interest_test_riasec&test_slug=holland-career-interest-test-riasec&target_test_slug=holland-career-interest-test-riasec&cta_id=cms_content_holland_career_interest_test_riasec&landing_path=%2Fen%2Farticles%2Fgaokao-score-major-shortlist-riasec-checklist&entrypoint=seo_cta), do not look at any single conclusion, but instead convert the results into "which majors' tasks should I verify?"

3. If you'd like to better understand your learning, communication, and decision-making preferences, you can take the [MBTI Personality Test](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types?entry_surface=article_detail_seo_cta&source_page_type=article_detail&source_route_family=article&source_slug=gaokao-score-major-shortlist-riasec-checklist&content_id=53&target_action=seo_cta_cms_content_mbti_personality_test_16_personality_types&test_slug=mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types&target_test_slug=mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types&cta_id=cms_content_mbti_personality_test_16_personality_types&landing_path=%2Fen%2Farticles%2Fgaokao-score-major-shortlist-riasec-checklist&entrypoint=seo_cta), but do not directly select a major based on your type.  
4. If you're still unclear about the differences between career interest tests and personality tests, see [Differences Between Career Interest Tests and Personality Tests](/en/articles/career-interest-vs-personality-test-differences).  
5. If you need a more comprehensive framework, refer to [Gaokao College Application Choices: Selecting a Major Using RIASEC, MBTI, and Career Interest Tests](/en/articles/college-major-choice-holland-mbti-career-test).

The value of these tools is not to provide a definitive "answer," but to transform vague anxieties into specific, verifiable questions. For guidance on the appropriate boundaries of use for these tools, refer to [Method Boundaries](/en/method-boundaries) and [Common Misconceptions](/en/common-misconceptions). Before taking any assessment, you may also review the [Data and Privacy Statement](/en/data-privacy).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### After Gaokao scores are released, what should you look at first if you have too many major options?

Hard criteria first: ranking, subject requirements, admission quotas, batch, physical examination requirements, and single-subject limits. Only majors that meet these hard criteria should be considered further for course study, personal interests, and real-world validation.

### After Your Rank Is Released, How Should You Narrow the List of Majors?

Start by narrowing down a discussion-worthy range using rank and enrollment plans, then eliminate majors that don't align with subject-combination requirements, have restrictions, involve long-term course resistance, are only appealing due to name, clearly conflict with real-world constraints, or cannot be verified. Do not initially sort all majors by interest tests.

### Can the RIASEC career interest assessment help me choose a major?

It can help, but it does not determine outcomes. RIASEC is better suited to help you observe which tasks and environments you are willing to engage with over the long term, and then translate those results into major verification questions. It cannot predict admission, employment, salary, or career success.

### Can MBTI Be Used to Choose a University Major?

MBTI can assist in understanding learning styles, communication preferences, and decision-making tendencies, but is not suitable for directly recommending majors. Treat MBTI as a language for describing preferences; do not equate the 16 personality types with a major-matching chart.

### Should New or Popular Majors Be Prioritized?

Not necessarily. A program's novelty or popularity indicates only that it warrants attention; neither means that it is necessarily worth enrolling in. You need to assess whether the school offers courses, faculty, laboratory facilities, practical resources, and pathways for employment or further education.

### What do I do when my parents' recommendations and interest tests don't align?

Don't argue over who's right. Include in the form the parents' concerns about stability, city, cost, and employment risks; also include the interest tasks suggested by the tests. Then verify through courses, interviews, open lectures, and real-world constraints.

### How Do You Decide Whether to Temporarily Exclude a Major?

If eligibility requirements are not met, there is long-term resistance to core courses, a preference for names over substance, reliance on popular narratives alone, clear family reality conflicts, or no verifiable pathway, it can be temporarily excluded.

### Is FermatMind an official college application system?

No. FermatMind is not an official college application system, does not predict admission outcomes, and does not replace the Provincial Examination Authority, Sunshine Gaokao, school admission rules, subject requirements, or the official application platform. FermatMind's test is only suitable for self-awareness and exploring hypothetical scenarios.

articles.content_md:
## Quick Answer: When Parents Don't Agree With Your Major, Don't Argue Who's in Charge

When parents and students have differing opinions on college major selections during the Gaokao application process, don’t immediately argue over "who understands the future better." First, use rank, subject requirements, enrollment plans, and other restrictions to eliminate majors that are not viable options. Then convert interests, concerns, and resistance into specific questions. Finally, evaluate each major through course schedules, program curricula, interviews, and low-cost experiences—categorizing them as “retained,” “under review,” or “temporarily excluded.”

1. **Pause first—don’t prove who’s right.** A parent saying “stability” and a student saying “I like it” are not, by themselves, enough evidence to put a major directly on the application.
2. **Begin with eligibility criteria.** Rank position, required subjects, admission quotas, physical examination restrictions, single-subject requirements, tuition fees, and city-based constraints determine whether a major is worth further investigation.
3. **Translate emotions into questions.** Phrases such as “I don’t like it,” “you don’t understand,” or “this major is more stable” should be reframed into verifiable, inquiry-based questions.
4. **Use RIASEC to assess task interests, and use MBTI only to supplement learning and communication preferences.** These tests are not part of the application choices system—they serve solely to generate actionable research questions.
5. **End by assigning each major a status—not a label.** Conclusions should fall into just three categories: retained, under review, temporarily excluded.

This article is not about making students win or parents win. Its goal is to transform family discussions from "mutual persuasion" into "shared verification."

## After Reading This, You'll Have Three Tables

This process produces three working tables:

1. **Hard-condition table:** whether the major can actually be applied for.
2. **Concern-and-resistance table:** what parents fear, what the student resists, and which evidence can test each claim.
3. **Decision-status table:** retain, verify, or temporarily exclude, with an owner and next action.

The tables are decision aids, not admissions predictions. All official rules must be checked against the current provincial and university documents.

## The 2026 Application Season: Why This Conflict Is So Common

From late June to early July, many families face simultaneously the release of scores, rank positions, online consultations, application choice decisions, major inquiries at universities, and discussions about new majors. Especially when terms such as "popular majors," "new interdisciplinary fields," "future-oriented industries," and "stable employment" are mentioned together, parents and students often reduce their anxiety into a single question: who should we listen to?

This background only indicates timing and does not imply an official relationship between FermatMind and any admissions agency. Final application decisions must still be based on information from each province's examination authority, university admission regulations, annual enrollment plans, subject requirements, physical examination standards, single-subject limits, and official university and college websites. FermatMind provides reference material for interest exploration and self-reflection; it does not predict admission outcomes nor replace the official college application system.

## First, Pause: Turn Emotional Arguments into Evidence Issues in 10 Minutes

Family disagreements often come down to two words: parents say "stability," students say "interest." Both of these terms are too broad. You need to break them apart first.

| Major | Parents' concern | Student's preference or concern | Verified Facts | Unverified Hypotheses | Next Steps to Verify | Current Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Computer science | High competition, high intensity, afraid of learning | Interested in programming, but worried about the pressure of mathematics and engineering | Satisfied with subject-combination requirement; ranking is within the scope of discussion | Whether you can accept long-term coding, debugging and project iteration | Look at the curriculum plan and do a 3-hour introductory programming task | To be verified |
| Clinical medicine | The family sees it as stable and socially respected | The student is concerned about the long program, workload, and hospital environment | The program length, physical examination, and subject-combination requirements need to be verified | Whether I can accept long-term high-pressure study and clinical internship | Check the admissions regulations, interview medical students, and understand the courses | To be verified |
| Journalism and communication | Students like to express, parents are worried about employment | Like content creation, don't like pure theory | Course direction has not been checked | Is real employment equal to "working as an independent online-content creator" | Look at the curriculum plan, do an interview or content project | To be verified |


**10-Minute Family Peace Process:**

1. Everyone shares only facts and concerns, without evaluating the other as "naive," "conservative," or "out of touch."  
2. Discuss only one major at a time—do not debate five majors simultaneously.  
3. First list "verified facts," then add "unverified assumptions."  
4. Majors lacking sufficient evidence are neither retained nor excluded—they go into "pending verification."  
5. At the end of each discussion, determine only what to investigate next—not make final decisions immediately.

> Quick use: If you have only 30 minutes left tonight, start by filling in the first five columns—"major name, parent's concern, student's resistance, next step for verification, current status"—and fill in the remaining columns tomorrow.

If you haven't completed your first round of major screening, you can review [How to filter too many majors after Gaokao scores are released?](/en/articles/gaokao-score-major-shortlist-riasec-checklist) after finishing this table. If you'd like to first understand how assessments function within Gaokao college application choices, read [Gaokao college application choices: How to choose a major using RIASEC, MBTI, and career interest tests](/en/articles/college-major-choice-holland-mbti-career-test).

## What This Article Does—and Does Not—Cover

This article addresses only one specific issue: **how to convert disagreements between parents and students regarding major selection during the Gaokao college application process into a clear evidence-based checklist.**

It does not provide a comprehensive re-interpretation of the complete RIASEC model. For a systematic understanding of the six RIASEC types, please refer to [RIASEC career interest assessment / RIASEC explained](/en/articles/riasec-holland-career-interest-test-explained). It also does not offer a full explanation of MBTI; if you'd like to understand how MBTI and RIASEC differ in their roles for career decisions, see [What to do when MBTI and RIASEC results disagree](/en/articles/mbti-vs-holland-career-choice). If you're still unclear about the differences between interest tests and personality tests, read [Differences between career interest tests and personality tests](/en/articles/career-interest-vs-personality-test-differences).

This article will not present any major as a definitive answer, nor will it estimate chances of admission, employment outcomes, income potential, or long-term development results. Final application decisions must still follow official provincial examination authority guidelines, admissions regulations, subject requirements, enrollment plans, score rankings, and official university information.

## Step 1: Remove majors that don't meet eligibility criteria


On the first pass, fill only eligibility and missing evidence. If an eligibility requirement is not met, temporarily exclude the major before discussing interests.

| Eligibility requirements to check | Where to check | What conclusions it may lead to | Precautions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Score/rank | Provincial Examination Authority, official score-to-rank table, and admission-threshold information from previous years | Majors that are obviously beyond the scope will not be focused on research | Information from previous years can only be used as a reference and cannot be regarded as this year's results |
| Subject-combination requirements | provincial application system, school admissions regulations, major subject-combination requirements | If you do not meet the subject-combination requirements, you will not be able to apply | Different provinces, years and institutions may be different |
| Enrollment plan | Provincial examination bureau announces plan, school official website | If the target province does not have an enrollment plan, the option cannot be included in the application | It depends on the year, province, and subject category |
| Physical examination / color vision / vision / height restrictions | Admissions regulations, physical examination guidance | There may be restrictions in some fields such as medicine, transportation, chemical engineering, teacher-education, etc. | Don’t just look at the major name |
| Single subject scores/foreign languages | Admissions regulations | Some majors may have requirements for English, mathematics, etc. | It depends on the specific terms of the school |
| Tuition / City / Campus / Accommodation | School official website, admissions regulations, family budget | Enter to be verified or temporarily excluded when the family is under too much pressure | Realistic constraints are also decision-making information |
| Major reassignment and transfer policy | School Academic Affairs Office, Admissions Regulations, College Official Website | You cannot default to "enroll first and transfer later" | There are usually thresholds, quotas and performance requirements for changing majors |


## What information must be taken from official sources?

Use official, current sources for:

| Information | Where to go? | Why you can't just rely on testing or experience |
|---|---|---|
| Application rules | Provincial Examination Agency, Admissions Examination Agency, official application system | Rules determine admission batches, application processing, admission, and submission procedures |
| School Admissions Regulations | School admissions website, Sunshine Gaokao and other official information portals | Regulations include restrictions, admission rules and special requirements |
| Subject-combination requirements by major | provincial application system, school admissions major requirements | If you do not meet the subject-combination requirements, you cannot apply directly no matter how interested you are |
