| Enrollment plan | Provincial enrollment plan and school release information for the current year | Enrollment in previous years does not mean enrollment this year |
| Physical examination and single subject restrictions | Admissions regulations, major descriptions, physical examination guidance | Certain restrictions will directly affect whether you can apply |
| Curriculum plans and courses | College official website, Academic Affairs Office, major curriculum plans | Major name does not equal four years of actual learning content |
| Major transfer policy | School Academic Affairs Office, Student Handbook, College Notice | "Enter and then transfer" is not a stable solution |


- Provincial application rules, rank information, and application model.
- The target university’s admissions plan and admissions regulations.
- Selected-subject, physical-exam, language, and single-subject requirements.
- Every major included in a university program group.
- Tuition, campus, program duration, joint-program status, and accommodation information.
- Curriculum, graduation requirements, and required practical training.
- Reassignment and major-transfer rules.

Social posts, short videos, test results, and family memory may generate questions, but they do not replace these sources.

## Step 2: Translate Parents' Concerns and Students’ Resistance into Testable Evidence


Write the concern without attacking the person. A concern stays “verify” until evidence supports retaining or excluding the option.

| Superficial statement | Possible real meaning | What to check | What is not recommended | Better expression |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Parents say "this major is stable" | Worried about employment risks, income fluctuations, and returns on family investment | Graduation destination, course difficulty, job types, urban distribution | "You are too old-fashioned in thinking" | "Let's first define stability: Is it employment opportunities, income fluctuations, or risks that the family can bear?" |
| Parents say "popular majors have many opportunities" | Worry about missing out | Enrollment popularity, course structure, industry cycle, personal learning costs | "Popular majors are pitfalls" | "Popular does not mean suitable, let's first look at what it will learn in four years." |
| The student says "I don't like it" | What I am resisting is the curriculum, environment, career picture or feeling of being controlled | Curriculum schedule, open classes, internship tasks, interviews with practitioners | "I just won't go" | "What I am specifically resisting are these courses and tasks, can we check together?" |
| The student says "I want to learn this" | Interest has not been verified by courses and real-life tasks | Curriculum plans, project assignments, graduation projects, introductory courses | "Just liking it is enough" | "I am willing to complete one low-cost verification exercise within a week before deciding whether to keep it." |
| The family says, "You also need to look at the city and cost." | Family budget, care costs, and living costs are hard constraints | Tuition fees, accommodation, campus, and city living costs | "You only care about money." | "These are realistic conditions, and I put them in the table together with major interests." |


## Step 3: Use RIASEC to See What Tasks I'm Willing to Engage With Long-Term


RIASEC does not match a person to one major. It makes recurring activities easier to name and verify.

| RIASEC clues | Questions that can be turned into | What should be verified | Don’t jump to conclusions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stronger Realistic R | Do I enjoy working with tools, systems, equipment, physical objects, or engineering tasks? | Experimental classes, engineering training, practical projects | "I can only choose engineering" |
| Investigative (I) is stronger | Am I willing to analyze data, models, causes, and complex problems over a long period of time? | Mathematics, statistics, experiments, papers and project tasks | "I must be suitable for scientific research" |
| Artistic (A) is stronger | Do I need space for expression, design, open questions, and creativity? | Portfolio, design classes, writing/visual/interactive projects | “I can only study art majors” |
| Social (S) is stronger | Am I willing to face people, communicate, support, teach, or serve on a long-term basis? | Real tasks such as teacher-education, psychology, nursing, social work, user research, etc. | "I am only suitable for dealing with people" |
| Enterprising (E) is stronger | Do I like organizing resources, influencing others, advancing goals, and taking responsibility for results? | Business, management, marketing, project-based tasks | "I must be suitable for entrepreneurship or management" |
| Conventional (C) is stronger | Do I like order, process, data, standards, and reliable execution? | Accounting, auditing, legal process, data governance and other courses | "I am not suitable for creative work" |


## Step 4: Course non-negotiables matter more than major names


Check at least four elements for each of the three leading majors: core courses, hardest or most resisted course, common assignments, and graduation requirements. A prestigious name does not remove a sustained conflict with central coursework.

| Attractiveness of major name | Course red lines that must be checked | Possibly exposed problems | Next step verification |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Artificial intelligence is very popular" | Advanced mathematics, linear algebra, probability, programming, machine learning, algorithms | I only like the name, not math and code | Find a Python/machine learning introductory course and try it for 3 hours |
| "Legal studies are stable and decent" | Read jurisprudence, constitutional law, civil law, criminal law, procedural law, and cases | Don't like a lot of reading, memorization, and argumentation | Watch an open law class and read a summary of a case judgment |
| "Clinical medicine employment is clear" | Anatomy, physiology, pathology, pharmacology, clinical internship | Long academic period, high pressure, physical examination restrictions | Interview medical students to check training years and physical examination requirements |
| "Finance offers high income" | Microeconomics, macroeconomics, accounting, statistics, financial engineering | Imagine the industry as high income, but don't know the course | Look at the course schedule and employment destination, and do a financial report reading exercise |
| "News communication is interesting" | News writing, communication theory, interviews, data journalism, internships | I only like to express and do not understand the rhythm of the industry | Do an interview or short content project |
| "Teacher education seems stable" | Education, psychology, subject teaching, trial lectures, internships | Like the subject but don't like the teaching scene | 10-minute trial lecture, interview with teacher-education students or teachers |


## Example 1: Parents Want the Student to Choose Computer Science, but the Student Fears the Course Load

**Scenario**: Parents believe there are many opportunities in computer science, students are curious about technology, but worry about math, coding, project pressure, and "competition."

| Steps | What to do | Conclusion in this case |
|---|---|---|
| Eligibility requirements | Check the ranking, subject-combination requirement, enrollment plan, single subject requirements | If the subject-combination requirement is satisfied and the ranking is within the discussion range, go to the next step |
| Parents worry | Worry about missing out on opportunities, employment opportunities, and income fluctuations | Rewrite "lots of opportunities" as: which directions, which courses, and which positions? |
| Students resist | Worry about the pressure of math and programming | No need to argue, just do low-cost task verification |
| RIASEC tasks | Whether you are willing to engage over time with Investigative (I), Realistic (R), and Conventional (C) tasks | See if you are willing to analyze problems, debug systems, and deal with details |
| Course red line | Advanced mathematics, linear algebra, probability, data structure, algorithm, programming projects | If you resist these for a long time at first sight, you cannot keep them just because they are popular |
| One week verification | 3 hours of Python introduction + reading a training program + interviewing current students | If you are still willing to continue after finishing, you can mark it "Keep"; if you have strong resistance, put "to be verified" or "temporarily excluded" |


**Communication Script**:

Student can say: "I'm not dismissing computer science, nor am I basing my decision on intuition. I'd like to start with a small project first, then review the course schedule. If I don't feel resistant toward the actual tasks, we can consider putting them back on the shortlist."

Parent can say: "My concern is about opportunities and risks, not necessarily making a choice for you. Let's first see if you can accept real coursework and assignments."

## Example 2: The Student Wants Journalism and Communication, While the Parents Worry About Stability and Employment

**Scenario**: The student enjoys expressing themselves, observing society, writing, or content creation; parents are concerned that majors are too abstract, employment is unstable, and future income may fluctuate.

| Steps | What to do | Conclusion in this case |
|---|---|---|
| Eligibility requirements | Check the enrollment plan, school level, city, tuition fees, and whether there are practical resources | Discuss interests and employment only after passing the eligibility requirements |
| Parents are worried | Worried that "liking to write" will not turn into long-term abilities | Check courses, internships, and graduation destinations, not just the name of the major |
| The student persists | Likes to express, but may not understand the pace of the industry | Needs an interview or topic planning verification |
| RIASEC tasks | Tasks associated with Artistic (A), Social (S), and Enterprising (E) interests | Are you willing to write, interview, communicate, organize information, and accept feedback for a long time |
| Course red line | News writing, communication theory, data journalism, interviewing, editing, internship | If you only like to express and are not willing to interview and be revised, the risk is higher |
| One week verification | Complete an 800-word interview draft + read the curriculum plan + interview a current student | If you are still willing to continue after finishing, mark it Keep; if only the idea appeals and the tasks do not, mark it Needs verification |


**Communication Script**:

The student can say: "I'm willing to do a real-world task once a week. If I'm unwilling to face interviews, revisions, and public feedback, I'll acknowledge that I should not keep this major on my shortlist yet."

The parent can say: "I'm not opposing your interest—I need to see how this interest can be transformed into a teachable course and structured tasks."

## Step 5: Place each major into three columns


“Retain” means worth further work, not guaranteed fit. “Temporarily exclude” describes the current evidence, not the student’s worth.

| Status | When to put it in | What evidence is missing | Next steps |
|---|---|---|---|
| Keep | The eligibility requirements are basically met; there is no obvious resistance to the course; the RIASEC tasks are interesting; family constraints can be tolerated | It is also necessary to compare the school level, city, major group and application preference order | Enter the candidate list and continue to compare institutions and major groups |
| To be verified | The eligibility requirements may be met, but the courses, tasks, employment, family budget or city information are unclear | Course schedule, curriculum plan, interviews, open classes, project experience | Set 1-3 days of verification tasks |
| Temporarily excluded | Eligibility requirements are not met; course red lines have been resisted for a long time; family constraints are obviously in conflict; no reliable verification path can be found | If there is new evidence, it can be reopened | It will no longer occupy the current discussion time |


## Weekly Validation Task List: Don't Decide Based on Chat Alone

> **Quick usage:** Assign one low-cost task to each major being verified. Do not run too many tests at once.

| Date | Verification task | Output | Judgment question |
|---|---|---|---|
| Day 1 | Check the admissions regulations, subject-combination requirement, enrollment plan, and physical examination restrictions | Record of eligibility requirements | Can we enter the discussion area? |
| Day 2 | Check the curriculum plan and core courses | List of potential course deal-breakers | Which courses have I resisted for a long time? |
| Day 3 | Watch 1 open class or introductory lecture | Experience record | Am I more interested, or do I want to escape? |
| Day 4 | Do 1 micro-task | Work sample, notes, code, or case summary | Am I willing to do it a second time? |
| Day 5 | Interview with 1-2 current students or practitioners | Interview summary | What is the difference between real experience and imagination? |
| Day 6 | Review RIASEC / MBTI results | Validation question checklist | Do the test results help me ask more specific questions? |
| Day 7 | Family Review | Keep / Needs verification / Exclude for now | What’s the next step for this major? |


## What MBTI Can and Cannot Do?

MBTI is not suitable for directly recommending majors. It is better suited to help understand: do you prefer independent thinking or discussion-based decision-making? When facing uncertainty, do you need more planning or room for flexibility? What kind of communication role do you naturally take on in a team?

| Tools | What can help in family discussions | What cannot be replaced | Which step is more suitable |
|---|---|---|---|
| RIASEC / Holland | Turn interests into questions about work activities and environments | Not a substitute for admission rules, course verification, evidence about skills | Verification of major tasks |
| MBTI | Describe learning, communication, and decision-making preferences | Cannot directly recommend majors | Discuss learning experiences and collaboration styles |
| Curriculum / curriculum plan | Expose real learning content | It cannot mean that you definitely like or dislike | Core-course verification |
| Interview/project experience | Supplementary real-life feedback | Cannot replace formal admissions information | Review of a major that still needs verification |


If you'd like a systematic understanding of the differences between MBTI and RIASEC, see [What to do when MBTI and RIASEC results don't align](/en/articles/mbti-vs-holland-career-choice). If you simply want to start with the test, you can use the [MBTI Test](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types?entry_surface=article_detail_seo_cta&source_page_type=article_detail&source_route_family=article&source_slug=gaokao-major-choice-parent-conflict-riasec-course-checklist&content_id=55&target_action=seo_cta_cms_content_mbti_personality_test_16_personality_types&test_slug=mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types&target_test_slug=mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types&cta_id=cms_content_mbti_personality_test_16_personality_types&landing_path=%2Fen%2Farticles%2Fgaokao-major-choice-parent-conflict-riasec-course-checklist&entrypoint=seo_cta) to supplement your understanding of learning and decision preferences.

## Communication Script: Replace "You Don't Understand" with "What Are We Investigating?"

**Students to parents:**

> I'm not choosing a major solely based on interest. I'm willing to thoroughly research the courses, restrictions, and real-world tasks associated with each major. Before any evidence is available, we'll label it as "pending validation"—neither retain nor exclude it immediately.

**Parents to students:**

> My concern is risk, not making decisions for you. We’ll first list out factors such as employment prospects, city of residence, costs, and course demands, then assess which risks are actual and which are merely imagined.

**Shared Agreement:**

> No major should be chosen based only on its name, popularity, family recommendations, or a single test result. Each major must go through at least three stages: eligibility requirements, non-negotiable coursework, and real-world validation.

## Next Step: Take the RIASEC Test, Then Hold Another Family Major Review Meeting

If you're still stuck in the debate of "I like it" / "You don't understand" / "This major is stable," the next step isn't to keep arguing—it's to turn your interest into a question.

- First take the [RIASEC career interest assessment](/en/tests/holland-career-interest-test-riasec?entry_surface=article_detail_seo_cta&source_page_type=article_detail&source_route_family=article&source_slug=gaokao-major-choice-parent-conflict-riasec-course-checklist&content_id=55&target_action=seo_cta_cms_content_holland_career_interest_test_riasec&test_slug=holland-career-interest-test-riasec&target_test_slug=holland-career-interest-test-riasec&cta_id=cms_content_holland_career_interest_test_riasec&landing_path=%2Fen%2Farticles%2Fgaokao-major-choice-parent-conflict-riasec-course-checklist&entrypoint=seo_cta) to identify the types of work activities you're most likely to engage with over the long term.
- Then enter your RIASEC results into the major evidence sheet and ask: What kinds of work would this major prepare me to do?

- If your family is still debating MBTI or personality labels, you can use the [MBTI Test](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types?entry_surface=article_detail_seo_cta&source_page_type=article_detail&source_route_family=article&source_slug=gaokao-major-choice-parent-conflict-riasec-course-checklist&content_id=55&target_action=seo_cta_cms_content_mbti_personality_test_16_personality_types&test_slug=mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types&target_test_slug=mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types&cta_id=cms_content_mbti_personality_test_16_personality_types&landing_path=%2Fen%2Farticles%2Fgaokao-major-choice-parent-conflict-riasec-course-checklist&entrypoint=seo_cta) to supplement learning about communication preferences, but do not directly select a major based on the type.  
- If you're already beyond Gaokao college application choices and experiencing overall career uncertainty, you can continue to explore the [Career Confusion Test & Reality Check Map](/en/articles/career-confusion-test-map).

## Next-Step Recommendations

**Main CTA:** First take the RIASEC career interest assessment, then convert the results into major verification questions.  
**Secondary CTA:** Use MBTI to further understand your learning and decision preferences.

This test is not part of a college application system and does not predict admission chances or recommend a major. It simply helps you turn vague interests into actionable, verifiable questions.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What do I do if my parents don't agree to my major choice?

Don't argue over who has the final say. Put parental concerns, students’ resistance, verified facts, and unverified hypotheses into a single table. Filter out eligibility requirements first, then evaluate interest and course options, and place any major assumptions lacking evidence in "to be verified."

### What to do when parents push you to apply for a popular major?

DO NOT simply rebut "popular majors are useless," nor should you accept "popular majors are more stable" without question. First examine the core courses, industry cycles, learning costs, enrollment plans, and actual job requirements of this major. If a major is popular in name but its coursework consistently conflicts with the student's non-negotiables, it should not be retained automatically.

### Who Decides: Parental vs. Student Preferences in Gaokao College Applications?

Application choices involve real consequences that must be shared by the family, yet students are the ones who engage in long-term learning and experience within a major. A more stable approach is not to decide who overrides whom, but rather to have each candidate major undergo the same set of evidence-based evaluations.

### What to do when a student doesn't like the major their parents chose?

Students should specify what they dislike: is it the course, assignment, city, pressure, or the feeling of being controlled? If they can identify specific non-negotiables, and then validate them through a schedule, open classes, interviews, and project experiences, their objection will be more persuasive than simply saying "I don't want to go."

### Can the RIASEC career interest assessment help choose a major?

It can help you translate interests into work activities and environmental preferences, such as a preference for analysis, expression, hands-on work, helping others, organizing resources, or maintaining order. It cannot replace admission information, nor can it turn any major into a single definitive answer.

### After Your Rank Is Released, How Should You Filter Majors First?

Check rank, subject-combination requirements, enrollment plans, physical examination requirements, and single-subject restrictions first to eliminate clearly ineligible options; then review core courses and curriculum guidelines; finally use interest assessments and real-world validation to determine which options to retain, require further verification, or temporarily exclude.

### Parents worry about employment and stability—how to include this in the list?

Break down "employment" and "stability" into actionable, inquiry-based questions: graduation destinations, industry cycles, urban distribution, proportion pursuing further education, job types, learning costs, and household financial capacity. Don't just state "stable" or "unstable."

### Is FermatMind an official college application system?

No. FermatMind is not an official college application system, nor is it an admissions agency. Official application choices shall still be based on information from each province's examination authority, school admission regulations, subject requirements, enrollment plans, and official announcements.

articles.title: Should You Accept Major Reassignment in Gaokao Applications? Start with the Unacceptable Majors in Each Program Group
articles.excerpt: Before selecting “accept major reassignment” for a university program group, sort every major in that group into three categories: unacceptable, pending verification, or acceptable. Then use coursework, eligibility rules, and family cost constraints to decide whether the reassignment risk is one you can accept.
articles.content_md:
## Quick Answer: Don't rush to click "accept reassignment" — first write out the worst-case scenario

Near the end of the application process, many families find themselves stuck on the same choice: students focus on their desired major, while parents worry about the risk of losing the admission opportunity—each believing they are protecting the future. A more stable approach is not to first debate whether "Gaokao college application choices should accept major reassignment," but instead to fully lay out all majors within the university program group and categorize them as **unacceptable / under review / acceptable**. Only after determining that you could accept the worst possible outcome among these majors should accepting a major reassignment become a viable option for discussion.

| Sequence | Don’t ask first | Check first | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Is this school worth applying for? | What application model applies to this admission batch in your province? | Do not import assumptions from another province |
| 2 | Could I be reassigned to another major | Which majors are included in this university major group | A complete list of majors in the group |
| 3 | Do I like these majors | Which majors fail eligibility requirements or involve courses and tasks you could not sustain | Unacceptable list |
| 4 | Are popular majors better | Courses, training programs, and work activities for each major | List to be verified |
| 5 | Whether to accept major reassignment | Could you accept the worst possible outcome? | Acceptable reassignment range |


In one sentence: **accepting a major reassignment isn't about being bold—it's about whether you're willing to accept the uncertainty of majors within the university program group.**

The rest of this article explains how to apply that sequence.

This article does not predict admissions outcomes, does not assess whether you will lose an admission opportunity, nor does it replace the provincial examination authority, the Sunshine Gaokao platform, university admission regulations, subject requirements, enrollment plans, or the official college application system. It simply helps transform a family’s heated debate into a clear, discussable list.

## The Real Source of Anxiety Is the Unseen Worst-Case Outcome

Many families aren't irrational—they're just focused on different kinds of losses.

| Common sayings | The real question behind them | Better ways to ask |
|---|---|---|
| "Declining reassignment is too risky" | Worry about receiving no admission offer or losing an opportunity | Which majors in this group can we accept? |
| "I will never learn this" | Worry about not adapting to long-term courses and tasks | What exactly do you study and do in this major? |
| "Only popular majors will have a way out in the future" | Worry about narrowing future choices | In addition to popular narratives, are courses and ability training suitable? |
| "Go in first and then change majors" | Treat the institutional path as a safety net | Are the rules for changing majors clear and can it be a non-guaranteed option? |
| "Everyone else applies this way" | Use experience to relieve anxiety | What are the rules in our province, this batch, and this school group? |


The student's concern is: I've clearly been aiming for computer science, clinical medicine, law, or teacher training. What if I end up in a major I don’t want to study? Would the next four years be extremely painful?

The parents' concern is: If we don't accept major reassignment, what if the major slots are filled after admission? Would that mean we lose our earlier chances of being admitted? Could that loss be worse than simply not liking the major?

Both concerns are valid, but family conversations often begin with accusations instead of concrete questions.  

Therefore, the first step isn't to persuade the other side—it's to break down "what we're afraid of" into factual questions: fear that declining reassignment could result in no admission offer? Then check the admission and enrollment rules. Fear of being assigned to a disliked major? Then review all majors within the department. Fear of being unable to complete studies over four years? Then examine course requirements, curriculum plans, and actual workload.

## Step 1: Determine Which College Application Model Applies

"Accept Major Reassignment" may vary in emphasis depending on different provinces, different batches, and different application choice patterns. Do not directly apply out-of-province experiences seen in short videos to your own application choice form.

| The patterns you see | Discussion points | What do you want to confirm | Pitfalls that are easy to step into |
|---|---|---|---|
| University major group | Whether to accept uncertainty within the same major group | Is the scope of reassignment limited to the group and what majors are in the group | Only look at the school name and favorite major |
| Major + institution | Whether each choice has been bound to a specific major | Whether each listed major is acceptable | List the majors you are not willing to study |
| Traditional college admissions or other rules | Subject to the provincial batch rules for the current year | Official rules on admission by major, reassignment, and loss of eligibility | Do not substitute last year's or another province's practice for current official rules |


This article primarily discusses the risk of "major reassignment" within a university program group. If your region operates under a "major + university" model, the focus will shift to: avoid listing majors you are unwilling to accept in your application choices, rather than worrying about major reassignment within the group.

A practical reminder: temporarily set aside what you've heard, past experiences, or what relatives have said. For formal evaluation, refer only to official sources such as the provincial examination authority, university admission regulations, enrollment plans, subject requirements, and officially published training information.

## Step 2: Don't just look at school names—copy out all majors within each group

Copy every major exactly as it appears in the official admissions plan.

| Major / major category | Your first reaction | Eligibility requirements | What to check for the course | What to check for the task | Initial status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Favorite major A | Want to go | Eligible / needs verification | Core courses, experiments, mathematics, writing, etc. | Daily learning and future work activities | To be verified |
| Alternative major B | General | Eligible / needs verification | Curriculum plan, specialization or major allocation | Whether the work would remain unacceptable over time | To be verified |
| Unknown major C | Unfamiliar | Eligible / needs verification | Curriculum and project training | Check student interviews or public introductions | To be verified |
| Major D that you strongly resist | Don’t want to go | Eligible / needs verification | Whether the resistance comes from the course itself | Whether it is intolerable for a long time | To be verified or unacceptable |


Do not fill the table from memory or from the university’s general reputation. The risk belongs to the actual group and current application rules.

## Step 3: A Three-Column List Works Better Than "Like/Dislike"

The three-column status helps you judge whether accepting major reassignment is a realistic option.

| Status | Judgment Criteria | Typical Sentences | Next Step |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unacceptable | The eligibility requirements are not met, or the courses, tasks, program length, costs, and risks of changing majors are unbearable in the long term | "If I were transferred, I would not be willing to finish my studies." | Re-evaluate whether to apply to this major group |
| To be verified | I just heard about it, was afraid, the name was unfamiliar, and did not check the courses and tasks | "I heard it was very tiring", "I don't like the name", "relatives said it was not good" | Check official information and actual course requirements |
| Acceptable | The eligibility requirements are met, the courses and tasks are not clearly unacceptable, and you can continue planning even if it is not the first choice | "It is not my first choice, but I could complete it and still see viable next steps" | Can enter the range of acceptable reassignment outcomes |


### University Program Group Table with Three Columns (Copy-Paste Ready)


| Major name | Parents are worried | Students are worried | Evidence checked | Current status | Next action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Computer Science | Fierce competition, fear of failing | Mathematics and coding pressure | Curriculum plan and course descriptions | To be verified/acceptable | Do a programming experience |
| Electronic information engineering | Also considered an engineering direction | Not sure about hardware and circuits | Courses include circuits, signals, and experiments | To be verified | Looking for students to interview |
| Materials category | The school level is good | The student strongly resists chemistry and laboratory work | Core courses include experiments and material properties | Unacceptable/to be verified | Will decide after another round of course review |
| Environmental studies | The family sees development potential | Don’t know what to do | Monitoring, management, experimentation, engineering | To be verified | Check the curriculum plan |
| Sino-foreign joint program | Good schools | Tuition pressure | Tuition fees, campuses, training methods | Unacceptable/to be verified | Check with family budget |

## "Unacceptable Major" Is Not Just a Harsh Label—It Requires Evidence

Many students say, "I absolutely won't study," and parents hear it as defiance. Many parents say, "This is also good," and students hear it as insincerity. What's missing in between is evidence.

You can break down "cannot accept" into five categories of non-negotiables.

### 1. Hard Requirements: Subject-Combination Requirements, Physical Exam, Single-Subject Scores, and Language of Instruction

Such issues should not rely on wishful thinking, nor should college names be used to cover them.

| Red line | Where to go for verification | How to deal with it |
|---|---|---|
| Subject-combination requirements | Provincial examination boards, enrollment plans, and school major subject-combination requirements | If you don’t meet the requirements, do not place it in the acceptable range |
| Physical examination restrictions | College admission regulations and physical examination related instructions | Restricted majors are marked in red |
| Single subject requirements | Admissions regulations, major description | Don’t rely on “it should be fine” if the requirement is not met |
| Foreign languages | Admissions regulations, major curriculum instructions | Confirm separately if you have special requirements |


Eligibility requirements are not interest-related. Once they are not met, they should not be included in "acceptable."

### 2. Long-term course non-negotiables: It's not about difficulty—it's about whether you can endure it over the long term

A course being difficult does not necessarily mean that a major is unacceptable. What truly matters is whether the core training within the major involves areas you have long resisted.

| The feeling a major name gives | What you need to really look at | Possible red lines |
|---|---|---|
| Artificial intelligence and computing sound cutting-edge | Mathematics, statistics, algorithms, programming, projects | Long-term rejection of code and abstract training |
| Clinical medicine is very meaningful | Anatomy, physiology, pathology, clinical training, a long program | Unable to accept a long program or clinical training |
| Journalism and communication seem expression-oriented | Interviews, writing, communication theory, content production, projects | Persistent aversion to sustained output and interview pressure |
| Materials science and chemical engineering have industrial value | Chemistry, physical chemistry, experiments, material properties | Clear aversion to laboratory work and chemical environment |
| Teacher education looks stable | Education, psychology, teaching internship, classroom expression | Strongly resists teaching and student interaction |


When reviewing courses, do not rely solely on the attractive terminology in the major's description. Instead, directly examine the curriculum plan, course offerings, laboratory and practical components, and graduation requirements. Only after reviewing these details should you decide whether the major is "unacceptable" or "pending validation."

### 3. Work Activity Non-Negotiables: Make "Dislikes" Specific with RIASEC

RIASEC does not decide your major for you, nor can it predict admissions. However, it helps you break down vague "I don't like" preferences into specific work activities and environmental preferences.

| Activities you reject | Things to be wary of | Verification issues |
|---|---|---|
| Long-term experiments, instruments, process operations | Materials, chemistry, some medicine, some engineering | Am I reacting to unfamiliarity, or do I not want to do it for a long time? |
| Abstract reasoning, mathematics, coding | Computers, artificial intelligence, statistics, some engineering subjects | Could I accept sustained training and project feedback? |
| Interview, expression, communication, coordination | Journalism, education, social work, management | Am I nervous or tired of this kind of task? |
| Standards, details, double-checking | Accounting, auditing, law, engineering management | Can I accept rigor and double-checking? |
| Persuasion, sales, resource coordination | Marketing, management, some business majors | Am I willing to face feedback and pressure? |


If you can't articulate why you dislike certain majors, start by taking the [RIASEC career interest assessment](/en/tests/holland-career-interest-test-riasec?entry_surface=article_detail_seo_cta&source_page_type=article_detail&source_route_family=article&source_slug=gaokao-major-adjustment-unacceptable-major-checklist&content_id=58&target_action=seo_cta_cms_content_holland_career_interest_test_riasec&test_slug=holland-career-interest-test-riasec&target_test_slug=holland-career-interest-test-riasec&cta_id=cms_content_holland_career_interest_test_riasec&landing_path=%2Fen%2Farticles%2Fgaokao-major-adjustment-unacceptable-major-checklist&entrypoint=seo_cta), and convert the results into actionable verification questions. Note: It is an exploratory tool, not a major matcher, and does not provide admissions predictions.

### 4. Realistic Costs: Tuition, City, Program Duration, Family Financial Capacity

Some family conflicts are not interest-based conflicts but stem from unaddressed real-world constraints.

| Realistic constraints | How to write in the table | Judgment reminder |
|---|---|---|
| Tuition and living expenses | Annual tuition, accommodation, and living costs | Sino-foreign cooperation and special projects must be listed separately |
| City and campus | Campus location, transportation, family distance | Don’t just write the impression of the school’s main campus |
| Program length | Four-year, five-year, or other extended programs | Long-term investment should be considered together with family planning |
| Follow-up training costs | Postgraduate studies, standardized professional training, qualification certificates, internships | Only write possible paths, not guarantees |
| Family care needs | Whether it is necessary to stay in a certain area | Realistic constraints can be carefully discussed |


Including real-world costs in the table is not "lacking dreams." This helps prevent discovering after admission that one cannot bear the burden.

### 5. Switching Majors Later Is Not a Low-Risk Fallback

“Enter the university first and transfer later” is not a safe assumption. Verify all six questions:

| Questions to check | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Does the institution allow major transfers? | Some projects or categories have restrictions |
| When may a student transfer? | Freshman year, sophomore year, and specific time points are very different |
| What grades or assessments are required | High grade points cannot be regarded as the default result |
| Do popular majors restrict transfers in? | The direction you most want to change may be the most difficult |
| Are there restrictions across colleges or programs | The rules may be narrower than imagined |
| Is the information from previous years open and credible? | If it is not disclosed, do not treat it as a reliable fallback |


1. Does the university currently allow transfers from this program or category?
2. At what time can students apply?
3. What grades, assessments, or prerequisites are required?
4. Are the most popular destination majors restricted or capped?
5. Are transfers across colleges, campuses, or program types allowed?
6. Is credible historical information available, and what remains unknown?

If the major is acceptable only on the assumption of a future transfer, classify it as high-risk and at least “under review.”

## What If One or Two Majors in the Group Are Unacceptable?

Do not decide from the number alone. Ask four follow-up questions:

| Question | If the answer is "Yes" | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Does this major actually fail an eligibility requirement? | Yes | Not within the acceptable range |
| Would I remain strongly averse to this major's core courses? | Yes | At minimum, classify it as high risk and requiring verification |
| Could I tolerate this major only if I later transferred out? | Yes | Don’t treat changing majors as insurance |
| Are there other major groups at the same school or alternative groups at the same level | Yes | Give priority to comparing alternative groups |


1. Is the major unacceptable because an official eligibility requirement fails?
2. Is the concern about central coursework and tasks, or only unfamiliarity with the name?
3. Would the student accept the major without relying on a guaranteed transfer?
4. Is there another program group or institution with a more acceptable worst-case set?


### Three Actionable Conclusions


| Situation within the group | What accepting major reassignment would mean | Next step |
|---|---|---|
| Every major is acceptable; a few still need verification but would be manageable | You can continue to discuss accepting major reassignment | Then review rank, application tiers, and official rules |
| Some majors need verification, but none is clearly unacceptable | Supplement the evidence first, don’t rush to make a decision | Check the courses, interviews, and experience tasks |
| It is clear that one or more majors are clearly unacceptable, and the worst outcome is unbearable | Accepting reassignment now carries a materially higher risk | Find an alternative group, place the group lower in the preference order, or reconfigure the application list |

## Two Family Scenarios: Turning Arguments into Tables

### Scenario 1: The Student Wants Computer Science, While the Parents Prioritize the University


The decision depends on the worst acceptable major in the group, not only the preferred computer-science option.

| Direction within the group | Student’s first reaction | Evidence to be checked | Possible status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Computer Science | Want to go | Mathematics, programming, project intensity | Acceptable/to be verified |
| Software Engineering | Acceptable | Courses, Tuition, Project Training | Acceptable/Pending Verification |
| Electronic information engineering | Uncertain | Circuits, signals, hardware, experiments | To be verified |
| Materials science | Strong resistance | Chemistry, experiments, material properties | Unacceptable/pending verification |
| Environmental studies category | Unknown name | Monitoring, management, experiment, engineering | To be verified |


### Scenario 2: Parents Recommend Medicine, Student Prefers Communication


| Directions | Values parents see | Students’ concerns | Facts to check | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Clinical medicine | Specialized training, social recognition | Long program length, high intensity, clinical pressure | Program length, core courses, standardized training, practical training | To be verified / may not be accepted |
| Preventive medicine/public health | Related to medicine, different paths | Don’t know the specific tasks | Courses, scientific research training, public health tasks | To be verified |
| Journalism and communication | The student is interested | Parents are worried about instability | Courses, work samples, internships, content production tasks | To be verified |

## A Communication Script for Parents and Students

If a dispute has already arisen at home, you can directly follow this format.

| Scene | Students can say this | Parents can say this | Common actions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Parents are worried about declining major reassignment | "It's not that I don't consider the risk of receiving no admission offer. I want to first see which majors in this group I really cannot accept." | "What I'm worried about is the loss of opportunities, and I don't have to decide for you." | List all the majors in the group |
| The student is afraid of being transferred | "I can accept alternatives, but these majors need to be investigated clearly." | "You can't just say you don't like it, you must make it clear whether it is the courses, restrictions or tasks that you don't accept." | Make a three-column table |
| Parents recommend a stable major | "Stability can be written on the list, but it also depends on whether I can continue to study for a long time." | "I want to make sure that you are not just relying on temporary interests." | Check the curriculum plan and real tasks |
| The student persists in their interests | "I am willing to use courses, projects and interviews to prove that this interest is not an impulse." | "If we can produce evidence, we will turn it from an argument to a verification." | Set a one-week verification task |


The core principle is simple: **Before evidence exists, treat it as pending verification; insufficient evidence warrants neither keeping an option nor exclusion.**

## If You Were Reassigned to a Major You Dislike, Do Not Equate It with Failure

Take four steps before drawing a conclusion:

| Steps | Specific actions | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Confirm the assigned major, campus, and curriculum plan | See what you actually study, don’t rely on the name to imagine |
| 2 | Check policies for changing majors, minors, double degrees, and changing concentrations | Review institutional pathways without treating any of them as guaranteed |
| 3 | Conduct a course and task verification | Determine whether it is unfamiliarity, anxiety, or long-term rejection |
| 4 | Design the observation form for the first semester | Give yourself a rational review window |

| Observations | Question to record |
|---|---|
| Course content | Am I temporarily unable to understand, or do I not want to learn at all? |
| Homework tasks | Which types of tasks make me more engaged, and which types of tasks make me obviously resistant? |
| Classmate environment | Am I affected by the gap, or is the major itself unsuitable? |
| Possibility of changing majors | Are the rules, grades, and time points clear? |
| Alternative paths | Are minors, projects, interdisciplinary competitions, and postgraduate pathways available? |


1. Confirm the admitted major, campus, and official curriculum.
2. Check current transfer, minor, double-major, and specialization policies without treating any route as guaranteed.
3. Complete at least one course or task-level verification.
4. Create a first-semester observation record.


Acknowledge the mismatch without treating the future as ruined and without pretending a transfer is certain.

## When to use the RIASEC career interest assessment?

If you've already listed your program groups but many majors still remain stuck in "I can't quite explain why I dislike them," you can use the RIASEC as a helpful supplement.

It can assist you in answering:

1. Which types of work activities do I tend to be most attracted to?
2. Which long-term tasks do I tend to resist?
3. Which majors require prior review of course content and actual projects?
4. Which "dislikes" stem from unfamiliarity, and which may indicate a fundamental mismatch?

It is not suitable for addressing:

1. Whether any specific major is definitely right for me;
2. Whether I will be admitted to a particular major;
3. What my post-graduation income might be;
4. Whether my future career will be successful;
5. Whether I should accept a major reassignment.

You can first take the [RIASEC Career Interest Assessment](/en/tests/holland-career-interest-test-riasec?entry_surface=article_detail_seo_cta&source_page_type=article_detail&source_route_family=article&source_slug=gaokao-major-adjustment-unacceptable-major-checklist&content_id=58&target_action=seo_cta_cms_content_holland_career_interest_test_riasec&test_slug=holland-career-interest-test-riasec&target_test_slug=holland-career-interest-test-riasec&cta_id=cms_content_holland_career_interest_test_riasec&landing_path=%2Fen%2Farticles%2Fgaokao-major-adjustment-unacceptable-major-checklist&entrypoint=seo_cta) and convert the interest results into "course and work activity validation questions." Then return to your three-column list and re-evaluate each major as unacceptable, pending verification, or acceptable.

If your conflict with parents primarily revolves around "who decides and how to communicate," you can continue reading [Choosing a Major When Parents Disagree](/en/articles/gaokao-major-choice-parent-conflict-riasec-course-checklist). If you'd like to further understand your preferences regarding study, communication, and decision-making, you may use the [MBTI Test](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types?entry_surface=article_detail_seo_cta&source_page_type=article_detail&source_route_family=article&source_slug=gaokao-major-adjustment-unacceptable-major-checklist&content_id=58&target_action=seo_cta_cms_content_mbti_personality_test_16_personality_types&test_slug=mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types&target_test_slug=mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types&cta_id=cms_content_mbti_personality_test_16_personality_types&landing_path=%2Fen%2Farticles%2Fgaokao-major-adjustment-unacceptable-major-checklist&entrypoint=seo_cta) as a supplementary tool. MBTI cannot directly determine a major, nor can it replace admissions guidelines.

## How does this article complement other Gaokao major selection articles?

If you haven't yet reached the "accept major reassignment" step and are overwhelmed by too many majors unsure of how to filter them, see the [Gaokao Score-to-Major Shortlist Checklist](/en/articles/gaokao-score-major-shortlist-riasec-checklist).

If parents and students are primarily stuck on differing opinions, refer to [What to Do When Parents Disagree on Major Selection](/en/articles/gaokao-major-choice-parent-conflict-riasec-course-checklist).

If you'd like to understand the RIASEC model, see [Explanation of the RIASEC Career Interest Assessment](/en/articles/riasec-holland-career-interest-test-explained). If you'd like to differentiate between career interest tests and personality tests, see [Differences Between Career Interest Tests and Personality Tests](/en/articles/career-interest-vs-personality-test-differences).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Should I accept major reassignment in Gaokao college applications?

That cannot be decided without examining the specific university program group. First, review every major in the group; if you could accept all of them, then consider whether accepting major reassignment could reduce uncertainty in the applicable admission process; if there are any majors that cannot be accepted, prioritize handling program group risks first.

### Will "accept major reassignment" lead to being assigned to a disliked major?

It can, but only if the applicable provincial rules, program-group structure, and university admissions regulations allow that outcome. The risk is conditional on those official rules and on every major included in the group, so review the complete group rather than only the preferred major.

### What Happens If I Do Not Accept Major Reassignment?

Depending on provincial admission rules and the university's major-admission policy, declining major reassignment may result in removal from consideration or prevent admission to another major in the group. This article does not predict outcomes; it only recommends that you first clarify which majors are unacceptable and which majors fall within the acceptable reassignment range.

### Can I still apply if I'm not interested in a major within the University Program Group?

You need to understand why the major cannot be accepted. If it involves eligibility restrictions, courses or tasks that are long-term unsustainable, and you're unwilling to accept being reassigned to a different major within the permitted group, you should proceed with extreme caution. If it's merely a lack of understanding, temporarily mark it as "to be verified" and make your judgment after thoroughly reviewing the course requirements and rules.

### Does the Major-plus-University Application Model Also Require a Reassignment Decision?

Provincial and batch rules vary. Generally speaking, "major + university" corresponds more closely to a single application choice mapping to a specific major or program group; the key point is to avoid selecting majors you are unwilling to study. Official determination shall still follow the rules set by the provincial examination authority.

### What to do if assigned to a major you don't like?

   
First check the curriculum plan, major change policies, minor or direction transfer pathways, then use the first semester courses and tasks to evaluate. Do not immediately equate the outcome with failure, nor should you rely entirely on the assumption that "you will definitely be able to switch majors" in the future.

### Can the RIASEC career interest assessment determine whether to accept a major reassignment?

No. The RIASEC can only help you observe career interests and work activity preferences, and is suitable for breaking down "dislikes" into verifiable questions. It is neither an admission-prediction tool nor a major-matching tool.

### Can MBTI Determine Whether a Program Group Is Acceptable?

MBTI can assist in understanding preferences for learning, communication, and decision-making, but cannot directly determine whether a major is suitable. Program group risks must first be evaluated based on eligibility requirements, courses, curriculum plans, and real-world constraints.

### Is FermatMind an official college application system?

No. FermatMind is not an official college application system, nor does it predict admission outcomes. Official applications should be based on information from provincial examination authorities, Sunshine Gaokao, school admission regulations, subject requirements, enrollment plans, and actual course details.

## Next Step: This Evening, Do One Thing—Turn "Unacceptable" into Evidence

If you're filling out a university program group, don't rush to select "accept major reassignment" yet. List all majors within the group and write one sentence of evidence for each: eligibility requirements, courses, tasks, costs, or risk of changing majors—what specifically makes it unacceptably difficult?

If you can't produce such evidence, temporarily mark it as "under review." Only after clear evidence exists should you decide whether this program group remains viable in your application choices plan.

When students cannot clearly explain why they dislike several majors, consider taking a [RIASEC career interest assessment](/en/tests/holland-career-interest-test-riasec?entry_surface=article_detail_seo_cta&source_page_type=article_detail&source_route_family=article&source_slug=gaokao-major-adjustment-unacceptable-major-checklist&content_id=58&target_action=seo_cta_cms_content_holland_career_interest_test_riasec&test_slug=holland-career-interest-test-riasec&target_test_slug=holland-career-interest-test-riasec&cta_id=cms_content_holland_career_interest_test_riasec&landing_path=%2Fen%2Farticles%2Fgaokao-major-adjustment-unacceptable-major-checklist&entrypoint=seo_cta) to convert intangible interests and aversions into concrete course, task, and environment-based validation questions. Test results are for exploration only and do not replace the college application rules nor predict admissions outcomes.

articles.title: Can You Study Computer Science or AI If Math Is Not Your Strength? A Course, Work-Activity, and RIASEC Checklist
articles.excerpt: Can someone who struggles with math still apply to computer science or AI? Start by identifying the specific math gaps, reviewing course requirements and real work activities, and using RIASEC interests to sort majors into three working lists: keep, verify, or set aside.
articles.content_md:
## Quick Answer: Can I Apply to a Computer Science or AI Major If Math Is Not My Strength?

Place the option in "Pending Verification" first rather than moving it directly to "Retain." Weakness in mathematics does not automatically rule these majors out, but current popularity is not a reason to force computer science or AI onto the shortlist. What needs to be done tonight is to break a vague question down into four pieces of evidence: what kind of math difficulty you're facing, exactly what your intended major studies, whether you can endure daily tasks, and whether you still want to continue after a 7-day verification period.

| Don’t ask first tonight | Write the evidence first | Where it ends up |
|---|---|---|
| Does weak mathematics rule out applying? | Is it because of gaps in foundational knowledge, weak abstract reasoning, or test anxiety | Type of mathematics-related risk |
| Are computing and AI popular? | Core courses in target school training programs | Curriculum reality |
| Does liking computers mean the field suits me? | Are you willing to write code, fix bugs, read documents, and work on projects | Work activity preferences |
| Could the gap be addressed over time? | Are you willing to continue trying during the 7-day verification | Evidence that the gap can be addressed |
| Should the option be excluded now? | Reasons for keeping an option / pending verification / temporary exclusion | Application-list status |


Many families hesitate not over the specific major, but over two fears that appear before the same application choices form: students fear being overwhelmed by math and coding throughout their four years of college, while parents fear missing out on popular fields like computer science or AI. Don't try to convince each other—first, write down the five items listed below.

This article does not predict admissions outcomes, guarantee employment, salary, or career success, nor does it replace the provincial examination authority, university admission regulations, subject requirements, curriculum guidelines, or the official college application system. FermatMind is not an official college application platform; RIASEC and MBTI can only serve as exploratory tools and should not be used to determine your major.

## What problem does this article actually solve?

After the application choices table is opened, computers and AI rarely emerge as major options—they often become a point of contention within the family.

| Dinner table arguments | Real questions | What to check next |
|---|---|---|
| If your mathematics is weak, you definitely cannot study computing | Which aspect of mathematics is weak? Does the core curriculum focus on triggering weaknesses? | Curriculum plan, proportion of mathematics courses, algorithm/data course requirements |
| AI is the future, so you have to apply | Does the target AI major focus on models, data, algorithms, or application development? | Course schedule, practical projects, graduation requirements |
| I like using computers, so a computing major must suit me | Do you like using computers, or are you willing to understand the system and write code? | Small code tasks, technical documents, project assignments |
| Weak mathematics can always be made up later | Are you willing to make up for it? Is it supplementing the foundation, or is it a long-term strong rejection? | Seven-day learning and verification record |
| Apply first and decide later | If the core courses are not suitable for you, is it easy to change majors? | Admissions regulations, major transfer policy, major group risks |


Students may focus on college life: Will I fail calculus? What if I cannot get my code to run? Will I understand algorithms? Is AI just a sea of formulas? Meanwhile, parents focus on opportunity cost: computer science remains popular, AI sounds promising for the future, not applying might mean missing out, and the student's current fear may simply stem from lack of experience.

Both sides are protecting the future, yet the debates often reduce to just two sentences:

- The student says: "I'm bad at math—I'll definitely struggle."
- The parents respond: "Computer science is still in demand—just push through it."

Both statements are overly simplistic. The correct approach isn't first deciding whether or not to apply, but instead breaking down the issue into four layers: **eligibility level (whether you qualify to apply), course level (can you actually learn it), task level (are you willing to engage with it), and real-world level (can it be validated in practice).**

This article is solely designed to help you complete this judgment matrix. It will not tell you which major is "best suited" for you, nor will it present any test as a major-matching tool.

## Layer 1: First Ask "Are You Eligible to Apply?" Not "Do You Like It?"

Before discussing math and interests, go through the eligibility requirements first. Many families skip this step and immediately argue over "whether to pursue computer science," only to discover that the target university's program group, subject requirements, health restrictions, single-subject requirements, or admission policies themselves need to be verified upfront.

| Eligibility requirements | What do you want to check | What will happen if you don’t find out |
|---|---|---|
| Subject-combination requirements | Requirements for physics/chemistry and other subjects in the target province, target university, and target major group | A preferred option may still be ineligible |
| Enrollment plan | Whether the target major will enroll students in the province/subject category, the planned number, and which majors are included in the major group | Mistakenly thinking that you can apply for a certain major, the actual major group risk is more complicated |
| Single subject requirements | Are there any special instructions for mathematics, foreign languages or other subjects | Ignore the hard limit and subsequent discussions will be invalid |
| Physical examination/color vision/vision restrictions | Are there any physical examination or color vision restrictions for specific majors | May be restricted in admission or affected in subsequent studies |
| Tuition fees/city/accommodation | Family budget, city costs, accommodation conditions | Majors can be studied, but the actual cost is unacceptable |
| Major change policy | Is it allowed to change, what is the threshold, and is the success rate public | "Enroll first and transfer later" may be only an assumption |


Only when there are no obvious conflicts in the eligibility requirements does the next level of inquiry begin: Is this direction worth further validation?

## Layer 2: Break Down “Computer Science/AI”

If your decision also involves the risk of reassignment within a university program group, first use the [Program-Group Unacceptable-Major Checklist](/en/articles/gaokao-major-adjustment-unacceptable-major-checklist). Computer science and artificial intelligence are not one uniform major. Compare the target program’s actual curriculum.

| Field | Common learning focus | Possible sources of mathematical or abstract demands | More questions to ask |
|---|---|---|---|
| Computer science | Programming, data structures, algorithms, system foundations, networks, databases | Discrete mathematics, algorithm complexity, system abstraction | Am I willing to understand the underlying rules instead of just using software? |
| Software Engineering | Requirements, development, testing, collaboration, engineering process, project delivery | Algorithm foundations, system design, project complexity | Can I accept long-term debugging, requirement changes, and collaborative delivery? |
| Artificial intelligence | Machine learning, data, models, probability statistics, linear algebra, optimization methods | Linear algebra, probability statistics, calculus, model derivation | Am I willing to face formulas, models and uncertain results? |
| Data Science / Big Data | Data processing, statistical analysis, databases, visualization, business problems | Probability and statistics, data modeling, mathematical interpretation | Am I willing to clean data, find patterns, and explain conclusions? |
| Network security | Network protocols, system security, attack and defense experiments, vulnerability analysis, rule awareness | Discrete mathematics, cryptography basics, system details | Do I like tracking anomalies, checking rules, and doing experiments? |
| Digital media/interaction/product-related direction | Front-end, design, user experience, product logic, content and technical tools | Code basics, interaction logic, some graphics/technical courses | Do I prefer a mixed task of "technology + expression + user problems"? |


This is an evaluation map, not an official classification or a recommendation list.

## Layer Three: "I'm Bad at Math" Still Needs to Be Broken Down

The same overall level of difficulty with math can reflect very different risks. A person who makes calculation errors but is willing to correct them should not be placed in the same evaluation category as someone who has long since developed aversion to abstract symbols.

| Type of mathematics difficulty | Common manifestations | University content that may affect | How to verify within 7 days | Conclusions that should not be drawn directly |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Slow in calculation/more careless | Can do it but easy to make mistakes, steps are unstable | Programming details, debugging, algorithm implementation | Do a small code task to see if you can patiently check for errors | Cannot directly judge that it is not suitable for computers |
| Difficulty remembering formulas | Struggling to memorize and panic when changing questions | Linear algebra, probability, optimization courses | Watch a concept-focused introduction and check whether the visual and intuitive explanations make sense | You cannot judge college performance based on high school memory alone |
| Weak abstract reasoning | Difficult to understand proofs, recursions, and symbolic relationships | Discrete mathematics, algorithms, machine learning | Watch a visualization of recursion, graph theory, or an algorithm and explain it back in your own words | AI/algorithm direction requires key verification |
| Unfamiliar with probability and statistics | Insensitive to distribution, expectation, correlation, error | Data science, machine learning, experimental analysis | Read an introduction to probability and statistics and do 5 basic questions | Data/AI direction cannot be kept on the shortlist based on popularity alone |
| Difficulty understanding functions/limits/rates of change | Weak sense of changing trends, continuity, and gradients | Advanced mathematics, optimization, model training | Look at intuitive explanations of derivatives/gradients to see if you can keep up | AI/optimization related courses should be verified carefully |
| Foundational gaps, with willingness to address them | I haven’t learned solidly in some aspects, but I don’t exclude making up for them | First-year calculus, linear algebra, programming | Study the missing foundations for 30 minutes a day for 7 consecutive days and record stuck points | It can be verified, don’t deny it immediately |
| Test anxiety | Usually I can understand, but my performance on the test is unstable | Final exam, timed computer-based work, and defense pressure | Take a time-limited quiz to record emotions and mistakes | The problem may be stress management, not just ability |
| Strong aversion to mathematics | Not just inability, but constant boredom | Mathematics classes, model classes, algorithm classes, AI basic classes | Look at the course catalog and 1 introductory class to record the degree of resistance | Be very cautious in the direction of AI/data/theory |


The key isn't "how high your current math score is"—it's whether you're willing to engage in long-term mathematical refinement, abstract understanding, and error feedback. If you are completely unwilling to engage with these demands, do not keep AI or computer science on the shortlist solely because those fields are popular.

There's also a more practical assessment: if you have a gap in just one foundational area but are willing to spend 30 minutes daily on remediation and document the reasons for your mistakes, this constitutes "verifiable risk." But if you consistently resist formulas, code, error messages, and abstract concepts—and refuse to engage with them—this is termed "core task rejection." The former can continue being evaluated through course review; the latter cannot be overridden by merely choosing a popular major name.

## Layer 4: Computer Science/AI Course Reality

What you're looking for isn't a general online "introduction to computer science" article—it's the specific curriculum of your target school. Focus on three key elements: course names, credit/hours and required course ratios, and prerequisites. Pay special attention to which courses are core requirements and which are merely elective.

| Course or module | What it tests | What it means to be "bad at math" | Pre-check moves |
|---|---|---|---|
| Calculus | Functions, limits, rates of change, abstract calculations | Foundational gaps will become visible quickly | Watch an introductory course on advanced mathematics and write down the first point you don’t understand |
| Linear algebra | Vectors, matrices, spaces, transformations | Common underlying tools in the AI/data direction | See intuitive explanations of matrices and vectors |
| Probability and statistics | Uncertainty, distribution, sampling, error | Central to data science and machine learning | Do 5 basic probability questions to determine whether you are willing to continue |
| Discrete mathematics | Logic, sets, graphs, recursion | Common foundation for algorithms, networks, security, and theory | Look at graph theory/recursion introduction and try to repeat it |
| Programming | Syntax, logic, debugging, and problem decomposition | Not just mathematics, but also a test of patience and error correction | Do a 1-hour small task |
| Data structures and algorithms | Abstract structure, efficiency, complexity | Weak abstract reasoning makes this especially important to verify | Look at stack, queue, recursive or search algorithms |
| Basics of machine learning | Data, model, error, optimization | One of the core pressures in the direction of AI | Watch an introductory lesson on "How to train models" |
| Operating system/network/database | Rules, system mechanisms, engineering details | Emphasizes understanding systems and tolerating detail | See if you like to understand how the system runs |
| Project practice | Collaboration, documentation, debugging, delivery | This often reveals what studying the major is actually like | Find a course project description or homework sample |


After reviewing the curriculum, don’t just say “there are many courses.” Instead, categorize them into three groups:

- **Willing to learn**: The course name immediately sparks further interest;
- **Acceptable**: Not exciting, but willing to put in effort;
- **Clearly resistant**: Reacts negatively or avoids core courses from the start.

If resistance is concentrated in core required courses, the risk is significant.

A simple approach is to print out the target curriculum and use three colors to mark it: green for courses you're willing to take, yellow for those that can be accepted with additional preparation, and red for long-term avoidance. If red flags appear only in a few peripheral courses, further investigation may still be warranted; if they cluster around key foundational courses like calculus, linear algebra, probability, algorithms, and machine learning, these cannot simply be dismissed with the phrase “I’ll just work harder.”

## Layer 5: Work Activities Are More Honest Than Major Names

Computer Science/AI is not just about math, nor is it merely about sitting in front of a computer. It involves a set of repetitive work activities over the long term. Whether you can accept these activities holds more significance than simply "whether I like computers" or not.

| Work Activities | Real Meaning | Possible Corresponding RIASEC Interest Clues | Self-Assessment Questions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Programming implementation | Turn ideas into runnable code | Realistic / Investigative / Conventional | Am I willing to check for errors line by line? |
| Debugging and troubleshooting | Read error reports, reproduce problems, and locate causes | Investigative / Conventional | If the problem is not solved immediately, will I keep investigating? |
| Algorithms and modeling | Abstract problems, comparison solutions, optimization efficiency | Investigative | Do I enjoy "why is this faster/more stable"? |
| Data analysis | Clean data, find patterns, interpret results | Investigative / Conventional / Enterprising | Can I accept dirty data and uncertain conclusions? |
| System maintenance | Understand rules, operate stably, handle exceptions | Realistic / Conventional | Do I like to make complex systems controllable? |
| Project collaboration | Requirements communication, version management, delivery iteration | Enterprising / Social / Conventional | Can I accept changing requirements, schedule pressure, and revisions to my code? |
| Product and user understanding | Putting technology into real usage scenarios | Social / Enterprising / Artistic | Do I care why users need this thing? |
| Reading English-language documentation | Look up information, read framework documentation, and read APIs | Investigative / Conventional | Am I willing to spend extended periods reading technical material that I do not initially understand? |


The RIASEC assessment does not determine whether "you are suited for a computer-related career." Instead, it transforms vague likes and dislikes into specific questions about work activities. If you'd like to first convert your interests into testable questions, you can take the [RIASEC Career Interest Assessment](/en/tests/holland-career-interest-test-riasec?entry_surface=article_detail_seo_cta&source_page_type=article_detail&source_route_family=article&source_slug=math-not-good-computer-ai-major-course-riasec-checklist&content_id=59&target_action=seo_cta_cms_content_holland_career_interest_test_riasec&test_slug=holland-career-interest-test-riasec&target_test_slug=holland-career-interest-test-riasec&cta_id=cms_content_holland_career_interest_test_riasec&landing_path=%2Fen%2Farticles%2Fmath-not-good-computer-ai-major-course-riasec-checklist&entrypoint=seo_cta). The results should be viewed only as exploratory clues, not as a decision-making engine for major selection.

## Layer 6: Three Demonstration Cases

   
The following three cases are neither major recommendations nor judgment templates. They merely demonstrate one point: even if someone has "poor math skills," their verification pathways may ultimately diverge completely.

### Case A: Average Math Performance, but Willing to Debug Code and Build Projects

Xiao Lin is not strong in math and often scores around average on exams. However, he is willing to work on small tools. When a website report fails, he checks the documentation; when code doesn't run, he first thinks "where's the error" before fleeing.

| Verification point | Better signal | Risk signal |
|---|---|---|
| Small code tasks | Able to complete and willing to fix errors | Errors immediately trigger strong frustration |
| Introduction to Algorithms | Can understand the basic ideas | Give up as soon as an abstract structure appears |
| Curriculum plan | Core courses are difficult but acceptable | Core courses are widely resisted |
| Interview feedback | After hearing about the real pressures, you still want to learn more | After hearing it, you just want to escape |


Such students should not be automatically disqualified from computer science simply because they're average in math. A more stable approach is to include software engineering, computer science, and cybersecurity tracks in the "under review" list, then monitor the results for seven days.

At this stage, continue evaluating computer science and software engineering tracks while verifying the course requirements at each target school.

### Case B: Attracted by AI's Popularity but Strongly Averse to Abstract Mathematics

Xiao Zhou's main issue is not a broad lack of foundational ability, but a long-standing aversion to abstract mathematics and model derivations. He feels excited by the popularity of AI, but shows clear resistance when encountering linear algebra, probability and statistics, optimization, or machine learning.

At this point, the claim "AI is the future" fails to address relevant risks. Fields related to AI often require greater tolerance for mathematics, statistics, modeling, and algorithms. Course offerings at target schools still need individual verification; however, if core courses in a curriculum trigger prolonged resistance, such programs should at least be temporarily excluded.

At this stage, place AI in "under review" or "temporarily excluded"; meanwhile, validate pathways toward engineering-oriented, applied, product, digital media, interaction design, or information management fields with technological intersections. This is an evaluation pathway, not a major recommendation.

### Case C: Enjoys Technology Tools and Product Work but Is Unsure About Pure Computer Science

Chen enjoys building websites, editing videos, researching tools, writing product documentation, and thinking deeply about why users can't understand a feature. However, he has limited interest in low-level systems, algorithmic competitions, and abstract mathematics.

Such students don’t necessarily have to choose between "pure computer science" and "no technical involvement." A more reasonable approach is to break down the goals: fields such as pure computer science, software engineering, digital media technology, interaction design, information management, educational technology, and data visualization all require varying degrees of technical skills, though their courses and daily work activities differ significantly.

At this stage, treat pure AI and theoretical computing tracks with caution. Application-oriented, product, interaction, and content technology paths still require validation against each school's actual majors and curriculum.

## 7-Day Validation Plan: Don't Decide in Your Imagination


The week may not produce a final answer. It should remove options supported only by popularity and identify directions worth deeper verification.

| Day | Action | What to record | How to evaluate it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Day 1 | Find the curriculum plan of a target school | The ratio of core courses, mathematics courses, and practical courses | Does the curriculum match what I imagined? |
| Day 2 | Watch an introductory lesson on linear algebra, algorithms, or programming | What made sense, where I got stuck, and how resistant I felt | Is this a foundational gap or a strong aversion? |
| Day 3 | Do a small code task | Can I diagnose the error and keep trying? | Debugging tolerance |
| Day 4 | Find a real course assignment or project description | Task format, delivery method, difficulty | Does my picture of the major match its actual coursework? |
| Day 5 | Interview a current student or practitioner | The most painful and rewarding part | Check assumptions formed from short videos or family slogans |
| Day 6 | Write a three-column list | Reasons for keeping an option, to be verified, and for temporary exclusion | Turn emotions into evidence |
